name: Computer Science
tagline: Thinking in steps, and teaching machines to think.

nodes.title: Step by Step
nodes.goal: Give clear step-by-step instructions.
nodes.kid_text: When you tell someone how to do something, say the steps one at a time, in order. To brush your teeth you first pick up the brush, then add toothpaste, then brush, then rinse. If you mix up the steps, like rinsing before you brush, it goes all wrong! Clear steps in the right order help a friend do exactly what you mean.

lesson_media.alt: Four numbered cards put tooth-brushing commands in dependency order: get the brush, add paste, brush, then rinse.
lesson_media.caption: Each step creates the condition needed by the next; reversing dependent steps can change or prevent the result.

lesson_media.title: Put the steps in an order that works
lesson_media.instructions: Move each instruction earlier or later, then run the sequence. The runner stops where the order stops making sense.

quiz.prompt: Making toast 🌅. What comes first?
choices: Get bread
Spread butter
Eat it
quiz.answer: Get bread
quiz.say: We are making toast. What do you do first? Get bread, spread butter, or eat it?
quiz.explain: Get the bread first, then we can butter it, then we eat.

quiz.prompt: Getting dressed 👕. What goes on first?
choices: Socks
Shoes
Tie laces
quiz.answer: Socks
quiz.say: You are getting dressed. What goes on first? Socks, shoes, or tie laces?
quiz.explain: Socks go on first, then shoes, and the laces get tied last.

quiz.prompt: Brushing teeth 🪥. Which step is last?
choices: Toothpaste
Brush
Rinse
quiz.answer: Rinse
quiz.say: You are brushing your teeth. Which step comes last? Toothpaste, brush, or rinse?
quiz.explain: Rinse is last. First the toothpaste, then brush, then rinse.

quiz.prompt: Bath time 🦆. What comes first?
choices: Fill tub
Get in
Dry off
quiz.answer: Fill tub
quiz.say: It is bath time. What comes first? Fill tub, get in, or dry off?
quiz.explain: We fill the tub first, then climb in, and dry off at the end.

quiz.prompt: Planting a seed 🌱. First step?
choices: Dig hole
Water it
Pick a flower
quiz.answer: Dig hole
quiz.say: You are planting a seed. What do you do first? Dig hole, water it, or pick a flower?
quiz.explain: Dig the hole first, so the seed has a cozy home.

quiz.prompt: Shoes on, then socks on 🤔. Fix it! First?
choices: Socks
Shoes
Hat
quiz.answer: Socks
quiz.say: Someone said: shoes on, then socks on. That is muddled up. What should go on first? Socks, shoes, or hat?
quiz.explain: Socks go on first. Shoes over socks, never socks over shoes!

quiz.prompt: Breakfast cereal ☀️. What comes first?
choices: Pour milk
Eat it up
Get a bowl
quiz.answer: Get a bowl
quiz.say: You are making cereal. What comes first? Pour milk, eat it up, or get a bowl?
quiz.explain: Get the bowl first, or the milk goes everywhere!

nodes.title: Sorting and Ordering
nodes.goal: Put things in order by size, color or shape.
nodes.kid_text: Sorting means putting things together that go together. You can line up your blocks from smallest to biggest, or put all the red ones in one pile and blue ones in another. Try sorting your socks by color, and everything looks tidy and easy to find!

quiz.prompt: Which is biggest? 🦐 🐟 🐋
quiz.say: Look at the shrimp, the fish, and the whale. Which one is the biggest? The shrimp, the fish, or the whale?
quiz.explain: The whale is the biggest of all three.

quiz.prompt: Red pile. Which one goes in? 🍓 🫐 🍏
quiz.say: We are sorting fruit into the red pile. Which one goes in? The strawberry, the blueberry, or the green apple?
quiz.explain: The strawberry is red, so it goes in the red pile.

quiz.prompt: Round pile 🔵. Which goes in? 🔴 🔺 🟥
quiz.say: We are sorting round shapes together. Which one goes in the round pile? The red circle, the triangle, or the red square?
quiz.explain: The circle is round. The triangle and the square have straight sides.

quiz.prompt: Which is smallest? 🐎 🐐 🐁
quiz.say: Look at the horse, the goat, and the mouse. Which one is the smallest? The horse, the goat, or the mouse?
quiz.explain: The little mouse is the smallest of all three.

quiz.prompt: Yellow pile. Which goes in? 🍌 🍇 🍎
quiz.say: We are sorting fruit into the yellow pile. Which one goes in? The banana, the grapes, or the apple?
quiz.explain: The banana is yellow, so it joins the yellow pile.

quiz.prompt: Square pile 🟥. Which goes in?
quiz.say: We are sorting squares together. Which one goes in the square pile? The blue circle, the white circle, or the purple square?
quiz.explain: The purple square has flat sides, so it goes with the squares.

quiz.prompt: Line up small to big. Who is first? 🐞 🐈 🐴
quiz.say: We are lining animals up from smallest to biggest. Who goes first? The ladybug, the cat, or the horse?
quiz.explain: The tiny ladybug goes first, because smallest comes at the start.

lesson_media.alt: Four mixed blocks become ordered from shortest to tallest after the rule sort by height is chosen, while a color grouping is shown as a different valid rule.
lesson_media.caption: A sort needs an explicit key. Height creates an ordered sequence; color creates groups. The same objects can therefore have different correct arrangements for different purposes.

nodes.title: Patterns and Rules
nodes.goal: Follow and make simple rules.
nodes.kid_text: A pattern is something that repeats in the same way, again and again. Red, blue, red, blue, red, and you can guess blue comes next! When you know the rule, you can keep the pattern going all by yourself.

quiz.prompt: 🟠🟣🟠🟣🟠 What next?
quiz.say: Look at the pattern: orange, purple, orange, purple, orange. What comes next? Orange, purple, or yellow?
quiz.explain: Purple comes next, because the colors take turns.

quiz.prompt: 👏👏🦶👏👏🦶👏👏 What next?
quiz.say: Listen to the pattern: clap, clap, stomp, clap, clap, stomp, clap, clap. What comes next? A clap, a stomp, or a wave?
quiz.explain: A stomp comes next, because two claps always go before a stomp.

quiz.prompt: 🍎🍌🍎🍌🍎🍎 Which one broke the rule?
choices: The last one
The first one
The middle one
quiz.answer: The last one
quiz.say: Here is a pattern: apple, banana, apple, banana, apple, apple. One fruit broke the rule. Was it the last one, the first one, or the middle one?
quiz.explain: The last one broke it. A banana should be there instead.

quiz.prompt: ⭐🌙⭐🌙⭐ What comes next?
quiz.say: Look at the pattern: star, moon, star, moon, star. What comes next? A star, a moon, or a sun?
quiz.explain: A moon comes next, because they take turns.

quiz.prompt: 🐶🐶🐱🐶🐶🐱 What comes next?
quiz.say: Here is the pattern: dog, dog, cat, dog, dog, cat. What comes next? A dog, a cat, or a mouse?
quiz.explain: A dog comes next, because two dogs start every turn.

quiz.prompt: ⬛⬜⬛⬜⬛⬜ What comes next?
quiz.say: Here is a pattern: black, white, black, white, black, white. What comes next? Black, white, or red?
quiz.explain: Black comes next, because black and white keep taking turns.

quiz.prompt: 🔺🔵🔺❓🔺 What is hiding?
quiz.say: One shape is hiding in this pattern: triangle, circle, triangle, hmm, triangle. Is the hidden one a triangle, a circle, or a green square?
quiz.explain: A circle was hiding, because a circle always follows a triangle.

lesson_media.alt: A written circle-square sequence is split into repeated AB units; the isolated unit predicts that a square must follow the final circle.
lesson_media.caption: A repeating pattern is generated by a unit and a rule, not by visual guesswork alone. Once AB is identified, the next position after A must be B.

nodes.title: Everyday Algorithms
nodes.goal: Write a recipe of exact steps a friend can follow.
nodes.kid_text: An algorithm is a clear list of steps for completing a task. Some steps depend on earlier ones: you need bread before you can spread jam, so those steps must stay in an order that works. Other independent steps may swap without changing the result. Good instructions name each action and object clearly enough for the intended follower.

lesson_media.alt: Four panels show two bread slices, jam spread on one, the slices joined, and the finished sandwich on a plate.
lesson_media.caption: Dependent steps must be included and arranged in an order that works.

lesson_media.title: Trace a sandwich algorithm
lesson_media.instructions: Run all four steps, then leave one out and see which later action can no longer work.

quiz.prompt: Jam sandwich 🥪. First step?
choices: Get bread
Spread jam
Eat it
quiz.answer: Get bread
quiz.say: You are telling a friend how to make a jam sandwich. What is the very first step? Get bread, spread jam, or eat it?
quiz.explain: You get the bread first, or there is nothing to spread jam on!

quiz.prompt: Bread. Jam. Eat. What step is missing?
choices: Put the slices together
Pour a drink
Wash the plate
quiz.answer: Put the slices together
quiz.say: Here are the steps: get the bread, spread the jam, eat it. One step is missing in the middle. Is it put the slices together, pour a drink, or wash the plate?
quiz.explain: You need to put the slices together before you eat it.

quiz.prompt: Cake 🎂. Which comes first?
choices: Mix first
Bake first
Ice it first
quiz.answer: Mix first
quiz.say: To make a cake, what comes first? Mix first, bake first, or ice it first?
quiz.explain: You mix first, then bake, and the icing goes on at the end.

quiz.prompt: Wet, soap, scrub and rinse your hands. What comes next?
choices: Dry them
Add more dirt
Put on gloves while wet
quiz.answer: Dry them
quiz.say: You wet your hands, use soap, scrub, and rinse. What comes next? Dry them, add more dirt, or put on gloves while they are wet?
quiz.explain: After wetting, soaping, scrubbing and rinsing, dry your clean hands.

quiz.prompt: Steps: pour milk, get bowl, eat 🤔. Problem?
choices: Bowl should be first
Eat should be first
Nothing is wrong
quiz.answer: Bowl should be first
quiz.say: The steps say: pour the milk, get the bowl, eat. What is the problem? Bowl should be first, eat should be first, or nothing is wrong?
quiz.explain: The bowl must come first, or the milk spills on the table.

quiz.prompt: Which one is an algorithm? 🤔
choices: A recipe for pancakes
A photo of a cat
A pile of blocks
quiz.answer: A recipe for pancakes
quiz.say: An algorithm is a list of exact steps anyone can follow. Which one of these is an algorithm? A recipe for pancakes, a photo of a cat, or a pile of blocks?
quiz.explain: A sufficiently clear recipe is an algorithm: its steps tell the cook what to do in an order that works.

quiz.prompt: Plant a seed: fill the pot, place the seed, then what?
choices: Cover and water it
Empty the pot
Put the seed back in the packet
quiz.answer: Cover and water it
quiz.say: To plant a seed, fill the pot and place the seed. What comes next? Cover and water it, empty the pot, or put the seed back in the packet?
quiz.explain: Cover the seed with soil and water it so the planting steps can do their job.

nodes.title: Ones and Zeros
nodes.goal: Count in binary; see how computers store numbers.
nodes.kid_text: Computers only have two signals, like a light switch that is either ON or OFF. We write ON as 1 and OFF as 0, and that is called binary. By putting a row of switches together, like 101, a computer can count and store any number at all! So every picture and song inside a computer is really just a big pile of ones and zeros.

quiz.prompt: Light is ON 💡. Which number?
quiz.say: A computer writes ON as one number and OFF as another. If the light is on, is it a one, a zero, or a ten?
quiz.explain: On means one. Off means zero.

quiz.prompt: One switch. How many ways?
quiz.say: A switch can be on, or off. How many ways can one switch be? Two, five, or ten?
quiz.explain: Just two ways: on and off. That is why it is called binary.

quiz.prompt: Computers use which two numbers?
choices: 0 and 1
3 and 4
1 and 2
quiz.answer: 0 and 1
quiz.say: Inside a computer, everything is made of just two numbers. Are they zero and one, three and four, or one and two?
quiz.explain: Zero and one! Every picture and song is a big pile of them.

quiz.prompt: Light is OFF 💡. Which number?
quiz.say: A computer writes ON as one number and OFF as another. If the light is off, is it a one, a zero, or a ten?
quiz.explain: Off means zero, and on means one.

quiz.prompt: Which one is binary?
quiz.say: Binary only uses ones and zeros. Which one is binary? One zero one zero, two zero two zero, or four three two one?
quiz.explain: One zero one zero uses only ones and zeros. The others use a two, a three and a four.

quiz.prompt: Two switches 💡💡. How many ways?
quiz.say: Two switches can each be on or off. How many different ways can they be? Four, two, or eight?
quiz.explain: Four ways: both off, one on, the other on, or both on.

quiz.prompt: Binary 1 0. What number is it?
quiz.say: In binary, a one followed by a zero means a number. Is it ten, two, or zero?
quiz.explain: In binary, one zero means two. Binary counts its own way!

lesson_media.alt: Three binary place-value panels labelled 4, 2 and 1 show ON, OFF and ON; the active values 4 and 1 are added to decode binary 101 as decimal 5.
lesson_media.caption: Binary place values are powers of two. In 101 base two, a 1 includes its place value and a 0 excludes it, so four plus zero plus one equals five.

nodes.title: Block Coding
nodes.goal: Sequence, loop and branch with visual blocks.
nodes.kid_text: In block coding you snap colorful blocks together to tell a character what to do, like build with LEGO. Put blocks in a row and they run one after another; wrap them in a loop block and they repeat over and over. An if block lets you make a choice, like jump only IF you touch the star. Snap the right blocks together and your character comes to life!

quiz.prompt: A loop block makes steps...
choices: Repeat
Stop
Skip
quiz.answer: Repeat
quiz.say: When you wrap your blocks in a loop block, what happens to the steps? Do they repeat, stop, or skip?
quiz.explain: A loop makes the steps happen again and again.

quiz.prompt: Blocks in a row run how?
choices: In order
Jumbled
Backwards
quiz.answer: In order
quiz.say: When you snap blocks in a row, how do they run? In order, jumbled, or backwards?
quiz.explain: They run in order, from the top block down to the bottom.

quiz.prompt: Block: jump IF you touch ⭐. No star touched.
choices: No jump
Jump once
Jump forever
quiz.answer: No jump
quiz.say: Your block says: jump only if you touch the star. You did not touch the star. Is it no jump, jump once, or jump forever?
quiz.explain: No jump. An if block only runs when the thing is true.

quiz.prompt: Loop: repeat 👏 three times. How many claps?
quiz.say: Your loop block says clap three times. How many claps do you hear? Three, one, or six?
quiz.explain: Three claps, because the loop repeats it exactly three times.

quiz.prompt: IF rain 🌧️ open umbrella. It rains. What happens?
choices: Umbrella opens
Nothing happens
Umbrella closes
quiz.answer: Umbrella opens
quiz.say: Your block says: open the umbrella if it rains. It is raining! Does the umbrella open, does nothing happen, or does the umbrella close?
quiz.explain: The umbrella opens, because an if block runs when the thing is true.

quiz.prompt: Which block makes a choice?
choices: If block
Loop block
Move block
quiz.answer: If block
quiz.say: Which block lets your character make a choice? The if block, the loop block, or the move block?
quiz.explain: The if block chooses. The loop block repeats and the move block moves.

quiz.prompt: Which block runs first?
choices: The top one
The bottom one
The middle one
quiz.answer: The top one
quiz.say: In a stack of blocks, which one runs first? The top one, the bottom one, or the middle one?
quiz.explain: The top block runs first, then it goes down the stack.

lesson_media.alt: A block trace starts at position zero, loops two one-step moves to a star at position two, then takes the true branch and jumps to position four.
lesson_media.caption: Blocks express control flow. A sequence fixes order, a loop repeats enclosed steps, and an if statement runs its branch only when its condition is true.

nodes.title: Parts of a Computer
nodes.goal: Input, output, memory and processor.
nodes.kid_text: A computer has four important jobs. Input is how you tell it things, like a keyboard or mouse; output is how it answers back, like the screen or speakers. Memory is where it keeps things to remember, and the processor is the busy brain that does all the thinking. Together they work like you: eyes and ears in, brain thinking, mouth talking out!

quiz.prompt: Which puts words IN? ⌨️ 🔊 🖥️
quiz.say: Which part puts words into the computer? The keyboard, the speaker, or the screen?
quiz.explain: The keyboard is input. It sends things in. The speaker and screen send things out.

quiz.prompt: Where does a computer remember?
choices: Memory
Screen
Speaker
quiz.answer: Memory
quiz.say: Where does a computer keep things so it can remember them? In its memory, on its screen, or in its speaker?
quiz.explain: Memory is where a computer keeps things to remember.

quiz.prompt: Which part does the thinking?
choices: Processor
Speaker
Keyboard
quiz.answer: Processor
quiz.say: Which part of a computer is the busy brain that does the thinking? The processor, the speaker, or the keyboard?
quiz.explain: The processor is the brain. It does all the thinking work.

quiz.prompt: Which shows you pictures? 🖱️ 🖥️ ⌨️
quiz.say: Which part shows you pictures? The mouse, the screen, or the keyboard?
quiz.explain: The screen is output. It shows things to you.

quiz.prompt: Mouse 🖱️ — is it input, output, or memory?
choices: Input
Output
Memory
quiz.answer: Input
quiz.say: You move the mouse to tell the computer things. Is the mouse input, output, or memory?
quiz.explain: The mouse is input, because it sends your clicks in.

quiz.prompt: Printer 🖨️ — is it input, output, or memory?
choices: Input
Output
Memory
quiz.answer: Output
quiz.say: A printer puts your picture onto paper. Is the printer input, output, or memory?
quiz.explain: The printer is output, because it sends things out to you.

quiz.prompt: Where do saved photos stay? 📷
choices: Memory
Speaker
Mouse
quiz.answer: Memory
quiz.say: Your photos stay safe inside the computer. Do they live in the memory, the speaker, or the mouse?
quiz.explain: Memory holds things so the computer can remember them.

lesson_media.alt: A keyboard sends input to a processor, the processor reads and writes memory, and a processed result travels to the screen as output.
lesson_media.caption: Input and output are data paths, not places where all computation happens. The processor executes instructions while memory holds instructions and data needed now or later.

nodes.title: Programming Basics
nodes.goal: Variables, loops, conditionals in a real language.

quiz.prompt:
A program runs these steps:

  count = 0
  repeat 3 times:
    count = count + 2

What is the value of count when the loop finishes?
quiz.explain: The loop adds 2 to count three times: 0 → 2 → 4 → 6.
9 is not greater than 10, so the else branch runs and y becomes 9 - 1 = 8.

quiz.prompt:
A program runs these steps:

  total = 20
  repeat 4 times:
    total = total - 3

What is total when the loop finishes?
quiz.explain: Subtracting 3 four times takes total from 20 down through 17, 14 and 11 to 8.

quiz.answer: Silver, since 8 misses the first test but passes the second
choices: Gold, since the branch written first is the one that runs
Silver, since 8 misses the first test but passes the second
Bronze, since the last branch runs once the others finish
Both silver and bronze, since 8 passes two of the tests
quiz.explain: The first branch that matches wins and the rest are skipped: 8 fails the >= 10 test, passes >= 5, so the chain stops there.

quiz.prompt: A beginner writes  if count = 5:  inside a program and it refuses to run. What is wrong?
quiz.answer: A test needs ==; a single = means 'store this value'
choices: A test needs ==; a single = means 'store this value'
A condition may not name a variable on its left
The value 5 has to be stored in a variable first
An if must be given an else branch to be complete
quiz.explain: In most languages = assigns a value and == compares two values, so a condition must use ==. Comparing a variable with a literal is perfectly ordinary, and an else branch is optional.

quiz.prompt: Two variables start as a = 5 and b = 3. The program then runs  a = b  and after that  b = a. What do the two variables hold at the end?
quiz.answer: Both hold 3, because a's old value was overwritten first
choices: Both hold 3, because a's old value was overwritten first
a holds 3 and b holds 5, because the values swap over
Both hold 5, because b takes a's starting value
a holds 5 and b holds 3, because the lines cancel out
quiz.explain: a = b replaces 5 with 3, so by the time b = a runs, a already holds 3. Swapping two variables needs a third one to hold the spare copy.

quiz.prompt:
A program runs these steps:

  total = 1
  repeat 4 times:
    total = total * 2

What is total when the loop finishes?
quiz.explain: Each pass doubles the value: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8, then 16.

quiz.prompt:
A program swaps two variables:

  a = 7
  b = 2
  temp = a
  a = b
  b = temp

What do the two variables hold at the end?
quiz.answer: a holds 2 and b holds 7
choices: a holds 2 and b holds 7
a holds 7 and b holds 2
Both hold 7
Both hold 2
quiz.explain: temp keeps a's old value safe, so nothing is lost when a is overwritten and b can be given the saved 7.
The even numbers between 1 and 6 are 2, 4 and 6, so the counter goes up three times.

quiz.prompt:
A program should greet each of five names but prints only one greeting:

  for name in names:
    greeting = 'Hi ' + name
  print(greeting)

Why does it print once?
quiz.answer: The print sits outside the loop, so it runs after the loop ends
choices: The print sits outside the loop, so it runs after the loop ends
greeting is overwritten each pass, so only the last one survives
The loop stops at the first name it successfully greets
print shows a value only the first time it is called
quiz.explain: Indentation decides what is inside the loop, and print is outside it, so it runs once with whatever greeting holds at the end. The overwriting is real but it is not the cause: moving print inside the loop makes all five appear.

lesson_media.alt: A short program loops over 2, 5 and 8, adds only values greater than 4, and traces total from zero to five to thirteen.
lesson_media.caption: Variables name changing state, loops repeat a block, and conditionals decide whether that block runs. Tracing each iteration explains why the final total is thirteen.

nodes.title: Data and Types
nodes.goal: Numbers, strings, booleans, lists.

quiz.prompt: You want to store whether a light is currently on or off, using a single value. Which data type fits best?
quiz.answer: Boolean
quiz.explain: A Boolean holds one of exactly two values (true/false), which matches on/off perfectly.
choices: Boolean
String
Integer
Decimal

quiz.prompt: In many languages, the expression "5" + "3" (both are strings) gives "53", while 5 + 3 (both numbers) gives 8. Why do these differ?
quiz.answer: For strings + joins the text; for numbers + adds values
quiz.explain: The + operator behaves differently by type: it concatenates strings but performs arithmetic on numbers.
choices: "5" and 5 are stored as the exact same thing, so this is a bug
For strings + joins the text; for numbers + adds values
The quotation marks are ignored, so both lines should give 8
Numbers get turned into text first, so 8 is really the text "8"

quiz.prompt:
A list holds five values:

  scores = [4, 9, 2, 7, 5]

Positions are counted from 0. What does  scores[1] + scores[3]  give?
quiz.explain: Counting from 0, position 1 holds 9 and position 3 holds 7, so the sum is 16.

quiz.prompt: A program stores a phone number as a number rather than as text. The number begins with a zero, like 0412. What goes wrong?
quiz.answer: The leading zero disappears, since numbers have no leading zeros
choices: The leading zero disappears, since numbers have no leading zeros
The number is stored fine but printed without its zero
The program refuses to store a value beginning with a zero
The zero is kept, since 0412 and 412 are different numbers
quiz.explain: A phone number is a label, not a quantity, so it belongs in a string. Stored as a number, 0412 simply is 412 - the zero is not hidden at print time, it was never there.

quiz.prompt: A program sets raining = true and cold = false, then tests  if raining and cold. Does the test pass?
quiz.answer: No, because 'and' needs both parts to be true
choices: No, because 'and' needs both parts to be true
Yes, because at least one of the two parts is true
Yes, because raining is true and it is tested first
No, because false makes the whole line an error
quiz.explain: 'and' is true when both sides are true; with cold false the whole test is false. Swapping it to 'or' would have passed. A false value is a perfectly legal result, not an error.

quiz.prompt: A class records the height of each of thirty students so a program can later find the tallest. Which way of storing the data fits best?
quiz.answer: One list that holds all thirty heights in order
choices: Thirty separate variables, one each
One list that holds all thirty heights in order
One string with the heights typed in a row
One number: the total of the heights
quiz.explain: A list keeps related values under one name so a loop can walk through and compare them; thirty separate variables cannot be looped over.

quiz.prompt:
A list holds:

  colours = ['red', 'green', 'blue', 'pink']

Positions are counted from 0. Which position holds 'blue'?
quiz.explain: red is 0, green is 1, blue is 2 and pink is 3.

quiz.prompt: A shop program stores the price 19.99 and the number of items bought, 3. Which types suit each value?
quiz.answer: A decimal number for the price
choices: A decimal number for the price
Text for the price, a whole number for the count
A whole number for both
Text for both, since they are printed on a receipt
quiz.explain: A whole number for the count. Prices need a fractional part; a count of items never does. Storing either as text would block arithmetic.

quiz.prompt: A program reads what the user typed with  answer = input('How many?')  and then computes  answer + 1, which fails. What is the fix?
quiz.answer: Convert the typed text into a number first
choices: Convert the typed text into a number first
Put quotation marks around the 1 so both sides are text
Store the result in a new variable instead
Ask for the number before anything is printed
quiz.explain: input hands back text. Text plus a number has no meaning, so the text must be converted to a number before adding.

quiz.prompt: A weather app records the rainfall for each of seven days and also whether an alert was issued on each day. Which pair of types fits?
quiz.answer: A list of numbers and a list of booleans
choices: A list of numbers and a list of booleans
A list of numbers and a second list of numbers
One number and one boolean
A list of text values and a single boolean
quiz.explain: Seven measurements need seven slots each, so both are lists: rainfall is numeric and an alert is true or false.

lesson_media.alt: Four panels apply type-specific operations: integer 7 plus 2 becomes 9, string 7 joined with 2 becomes 72, a Boolean conjunction is false, and a list appends an item.
lesson_media.caption: A type constrains representation and valid operations. The same plus-like notation can mean arithmetic for numbers and concatenation for strings, so values must not be interpreted by appearance alone.

nodes.title: Functions
nodes.goal: Package steps into reusable functions.

quiz.prompt:
A function is defined as:

  function double(n):
    return n + n

What does double(double(3)) return?
quiz.explain: The inner double(3) returns 6, then double(6) returns 12.

quiz.prompt: What is the main advantage of packaging repeated steps into a function you call by name?
quiz.answer: You write the logic once and reuse it everywhere it is needed
quiz.explain: Functions capture reusable steps in one definition, so you avoid duplication and fix bugs in a single spot.
choices: You write the logic once and reuse it everywhere it is needed
Functions make a program run faster than repeating the code
It lets the computer skip steps it has already run once before
Code inside a function is checked for mistakes before it runs

quiz.explain: The inner call runs first: add3(4) gives 7, and twice(7) doubles it to 14.

quiz.prompt: A function that works out an area finishes with  print(total)  instead of  return total. The caller writes  x = area(5)  and then tries to use x. What goes wrong?
quiz.answer: x gets nothing usable, because the value was shown, not handed back
choices: x gets nothing usable, because the value was shown, not handed back
x holds the correct total, since printing also stores the value
The function refuses to run without a return line in it
x holds the text that was printed rather than the number
quiz.explain: print puts a value on the screen; return hands it back to whatever called the function. Without return, the caller receives nothing.

quiz.prompt: A function greet(name) prints a hello message using name. The program calls greet("Sam") and later greet("Ada"). What job does name do inside the function?
quiz.answer: It stands in for whichever value the caller supplies that time
choices: It stands in for whichever value the caller supplies that time
It is a fixed value chosen when the function was written
It holds both names at once so the message can list them
It is the name of the function, repeated inside the body
quiz.explain: A parameter is a placeholder: each call fills it with that call's value, so one body serves Sam and Ada alike.

quiz.prompt: A 200-line program draws a house by repeating the same 12 lines for each window. A teacher suggests moving those 12 lines into a function drawWindow(). Which benefit is the strongest reason?
quiz.answer: A fix to the window code happens in one place
choices: A fix to the window code happens in one place
The computer skips drawing it has done before
The program uses less memory while it is running
Each window can be a different colour without new code
quiz.explain: Naming a repeated block once means later changes and bug fixes are made in a single definition rather than in every copy.
The inner call runs first: addTen(30) is 40, and half of 40 is 20.

quiz.prompt:
A function is defined as:

  function label(name, count):
    return count + ' ' + name

What does label('apples', '3') return?
quiz.answer: 3 apples
choices: 3 apples
apples 3
apples3
An error, because the values are the wrong way round
quiz.explain: Arguments fill the parameters in order, so name is 'apples' and count is '3'; the function joins count first.

quiz.prompt:
A function is defined as:

  function tally():
    total = 0
    total = total + 1
    return total

The program calls tally() three times. What does the third call return?
quiz.answer: 1, since total starts again at 0 on every call
choices: 1, since total starts again at 0 on every call
3, because total keeps counting up across calls
2, because the first call does not count
0, because the change is thrown away
quiz.explain: A variable created inside a function is made fresh each time the function runs and disappears when it ends.

quiz.prompt: Why is a function that returns its result more useful than one that only prints it?
quiz.answer: A returned value comes back to the caller, who can store it, test it or pass it into another function, while printed text only reaches the screen and cannot be reused by the program.
quiz.explain: Printing shows a result to a person; returning hands it back to the program so later steps can use it.

lesson_media.alt: The function double returns x times 2 and is called twice; the trace substitutes 3 to produce 6 and 5 to produce 10 without duplicating the function body.
lesson_media.caption: A function packages a parameterized computation. Each call binds a fresh argument to x, evaluates the same body, and returns a result to the caller.

nodes.title: Finding Bugs
nodes.goal: Read errors; test and fix your code.

quiz.prompt:
Your program should print the numbers 1 through 5, but it prints 1 through 4. The loop is written:

  for i from 1 to 4:
    print(i)

What is the best fix?
quiz.answer: Change the loop range to go from 1 to 5
quiz.explain: The loop stops at 4, so extending its range to 5 makes it print the missing final number.
choices: Change the loop to start at 0, not at 1
Add a second print(i) call inside the loop
Change the loop range to go from 1 to 5
Delete the print statement from the loop

quiz.prompt: A program crashes with the message "Error on line 12: undefined variable 'totl'". What is the most likely cause?
quiz.answer: A typo: 'totl' was probably meant to be 'total'
quiz.explain: An 'undefined variable' error for a name one letter away from 'total' points to a spelling mistake. The other two code explanations do produce this error in general - which is why the giveaway here is the near-miss spelling, not the error text alone.
choices: A typo: 'totl' was probably meant to be 'total'
'totl' was assigned inside a branch that never ran
'totl' was spelled correctly but declared after line 12
The computer had run out of memory at that moment

quiz.explain: The inner loop runs 3 times for each of the 6 players, so 18 cards go out - six short, because the inner range should reach 4.

quiz.prompt: Program A stops at once with "missing closing bracket on line 6". Program B runs to the end but reports an average of 0. What kind of fault does each have?
quiz.answer: A has a syntax error; B has a logic error
choices: A has a syntax error; B has a logic error
A has a logic error; B has a syntax error
Both are syntax errors, since both give a wrong result
Both are logic errors, since the computer did as it was told
quiz.explain: A syntax error breaks the rules of the language so the program will not start; a logic error runs happily and computes the wrong thing.

quiz.prompt: A program gives the wrong total and you have no idea which of its 40 lines is at fault. Which step narrows the search fastest?
quiz.answer: Print the running total at a few points to see where it goes wrong
choices: Print the running total at a few points to see where it goes wrong
Read the 40 lines from the top until the mistake stands out
Rewrite the calculation in a way you find easier to follow
Test the program on a much larger set of numbers
quiz.explain: Printing a value partway through splits the program into a good half and a bad half, so each run halves the region where the bug can hide. Re-reading and rewriting search the whole program at once, and bigger input makes a wrong total harder to check, not easier.

quiz.prompt: A program stops with "cannot convert 'eight' to a number" after a user types a word where digits were expected. Which fix handles the problem properly?
quiz.answer: Check what was typed and ask again when it is not a number
choices: Check what was typed and ask again when it is not a number
Catch the error and carry on with a total of zero
Tell the user in the prompt that digits are required
Convert the word to a number with a longer list of words
quiz.explain: The program has to cope with input it did not expect. Swallowing the error hides a wrong answer, a clearer prompt is advice rather than a check, and spelling out number words solves one case of an unbounded problem.
The outer loop runs 10 times and the inner loop 2 times each, so print runs 10 x 2 = 20 times.

quiz.prompt: A program works on your laptop but crashes for a friend who typed a name containing a space. What is the most useful next step?
quiz.answer: Run your own copy with that exact input
choices: Run your own copy with that exact input
Read the code looking for the place a space could matter
Add a check that rejects names containing a space
Ask your friend to send a screenshot of the error
quiz.explain: So the crash happens for you. A bug you can reproduce on demand is a bug you can study. Reading is guesswork until you know where to look, a screenshot gives one line of a stack you cannot explore, and rejecting spaces removes a legitimate name instead of the fault.

quiz.prompt: A list holds 5 items. The code loops i from 0 to 5 and reads list[i] each time. What happens?
quiz.answer: It fails at i = 5
choices: It fails at i = 5
It fails at i = 0, since counting starts at 1
It works and prints all five items
It loops forever
quiz.explain: Since the last position is 4. With positions counted from 0, a list of 5 items uses 0 to 4. Asking for position 5 goes past the end.

quiz.prompt: A program computes an average as  total / count  and crashes with 'division by zero' whenever the list is empty. Which fix is the right one?
quiz.answer: Check for an empty list first and report that no average exists
choices: Check for an empty list first and report that no average exists
Return zero whenever the list turns out to be empty
Set count to 1 whenever the list is empty
Add a single zero to the list before dividing
quiz.explain: An empty list has no average, so the honest fix is to detect that case. The other three all invent an answer of zero, which the caller cannot tell apart from a genuine average of zero.

lesson_media.alt: A failing test for the three-item list A B C traces indexes zero through three, exposes index three as out of range, and fixes a loop bound from less-than-or-equal to strictly less-than length.
lesson_media.caption: Debugging links a reproducible failure to the smallest causal state. A length-three list has valid indexes zero, one and two; stopping before length removes the off-by-one access.

nodes.title: How the Internet Works
nodes.goal: Networks, the web, and staying safe online.

quiz.prompt: You type a website address into your browser and a page appears. Which best describes what happened?
quiz.answer: Your device asked another computer (a server) for the page
quiz.explain: The web works by clients requesting resources from servers, which reply with the content. The address only says where to ask; providers may cache pages on the way, but they are not where the page comes from.
choices: Your device generated the page without contacting anything
Your device asked another computer (a server) for the page
The address itself contains the page, which the browser unpacks
Your internet provider keeps a copy of every page and sent it

quiz.prompt: A message pops up saying "Your account is locked! Click here and enter your password to unlock it." from an address you don't recognize. What is the safest response?
quiz.answer: Do not click the link; check by visiting the real site
quiz.explain: Unexpected urgent messages asking for passwords are classic phishing. Replying confirms your address is live, and merely opening the link tells the sender the same thing, so the safe move is to reach the site by an address you already trust.
choices: Click the link and enter your password to stop the deletion
Reply to the message asking them to confirm it is genuine
Open the link but type nothing, just to see where it goes
Do not click the link; check by visiting the real site

quiz.prompt: A 12 megabyte file is split into packets that each carry 1.5 megabytes. How many packets are sent?
quiz.explain: 12 divided by 1.5 is 8, so the file travels as 8 packets that the receiver puts back together.

quiz.prompt: You type example.com and your computer first asks another machine to look up a number like 93.184.216.34. Why is that step needed?
quiz.answer: Machines route messages by number, so the name has to be translated
choices: Machines route messages by number, so the name has to be translated
The number is a password that proves you may visit the site
Names change too often, so the number is stored as a backup
The lookup checks whether the website is safe to open
quiz.explain: The domain name system turns a name people can remember into the numeric address that routers actually use to deliver packets.

quiz.prompt: A photo you send is broken into 40 packets. Some travel by different routes and arrive out of order. What happens next?
quiz.answer: The receiver reorders them using their numbers
choices: The receiver reorders them using their numbers
The packets are thrown away and the photo is sent again
The photo arrives scrambled, with its parts in wrong places
The routers hold every packet until the whole set is ready
quiz.explain: Each packet carries a sequence number, so the receiver can rebuild the original file whatever route or order the packets took.

quiz.prompt: Two sites ask for your password. One address starts with https:// and shows a padlock; the other starts with http://. What does the padlock actually promise?
quiz.answer: The traffic is scrambled between you and that site
choices: The traffic is scrambled between you and that site
The people who run the site are honest and trustworthy
The site has been checked and approved by a government
Your password is stored safely once the site receives it
quiz.explain: HTTPS encrypts data on its way and confirms you reached the named site; it says nothing about whether that site's owners can be trusted.

quiz.prompt: A page is 2.4 megabytes and your connection moves 0.6 megabytes each second. How many seconds does the download take?
quiz.explain: 2.4 divided by 0.6 is 4 seconds.

quiz.prompt: A friend says a website 'lives inside your browser'. Where do a site's files actually sit before you see them?
quiz.answer: On a server, which sends a copy when your browser asks
choices: On a server, which sends a copy when your browser asks
Inside the browser, which downloads every site when it is installed
On the router in your home
Nowhere until you type the address, when the page is made fresh for you
quiz.explain: Your browser is a reader, not a library. The files sit on a server until a request brings a copy to your device.

quiz.prompt: A game asks for your home address so it can 'send you a prize'. What is the safest thing to do?
quiz.answer: Do not give it, and tell a trusted adult
choices: Do not give it, and tell a trusted adult
Give it, since the game already knows your name
Give it as long as the page shows a padlock
Give it but leave off the house number
quiz.explain: A padlock only means the message is scrambled on the way; it says nothing about whether the receiver can be trusted. A partial address is still your address, and a name the game already has does not make more data safe to add.

quiz.prompt: Your phone shows full Wi-Fi bars but no page will load. What does that tell you?
quiz.answer: The link to your router works, but the router's link onward may not
choices: The link to your router works, but the router's link onward may not
Full bars guarantee the internet works, so the phone must be broken
The signal is strong but too slow to carry a whole page
The site is refusing your phone while allowing other devices
quiz.explain: The bars measure the hop between phone and router only. Everything beyond the router is a separate connection, which is why no page loads at all rather than loading slowly or only from one site.

lesson_media.alt: A browser asks DNS for example.org's address, opens an encrypted HTTPS connection to that server, sends a request, and receives the page response.
lesson_media.caption: The web runs over networks: DNS maps a name to an address, routing carries packets, and HTTPS authenticates the site and encrypts data in transit. Encryption does not make every site trustworthy.

nodes.title: Fast and Slow Programs
nodes.goal: Notice that some methods are much faster than others.

quiz.prompt: To find a name in a sorted phone book, Method A checks every page from the front one by one. Method B opens to the middle and throws away the half that can't contain the name, then repeats. For a very large book, which is faster and why?
quiz.answer: Method B, because halving the range needs fewer checks
quiz.explain: Repeatedly halving (binary search) needs only about log-many steps, hugely fewer than checking every page.
choices: Method A, because opening to the middle wastes many steps
Method A, because it works through the pages in order
They are equally fast since both eventually find the name
Method B, because halving the range needs fewer checks

quiz.prompt: Method A checks items one at a time from the start. In the worst case, how many checks does it need to find an item in a list of 1000 items?
quiz.explain: Checking one at a time, the item could be last, so the worst case is all 1000 checks.

quiz.prompt: A sorted list holds 64 items and a program repeatedly throws away half of what is left. How many halvings take it from 64 items down to 1?
quiz.explain: 64 to 32 to 16 to 8 to 4 to 2 to 1 is six halvings, which is why halving beats checking one item at a time.

quiz.prompt: A program compares every pair of names in a list to find duplicates. With 100 names it does about 10,000 comparisons. Roughly how many with 200 names?
quiz.answer: About 40,000, because doubling the list quadruples the pairs
choices: About 40,000, because doubling the list quadruples the pairs
About 20,000, because the list is twice as long
About 10,100, since just the new names add work
About 200, because the name count sets the work
quiz.explain: The number of pairs grows with the square of the list length, so twice as many names means four times as many comparisons.

quiz.prompt: A game finds a card in a sorted pile by halving the pile each time. Going from 8 cards to 16 cards adds how much work?
quiz.answer: One extra check
choices: One extra check
Twice as many checks
Eight checks
Four times as many checks
quiz.explain: Each doubling of the pile adds a single halving step: 8 cards need about 3 checks and 16 need about 4.

quiz.prompt: Two programs handle a list of 1,000 names. Program P prints the first name. Program Q compares every name with every other name. How does the work of each change if the list grows to 10,000 names?
quiz.answer: P stays the same; Q grows about a hundred times
choices: P stays the same; Q grows about a hundred times
Both grow about ten times, matching the list
P grows ten times; Q grows ten times as well
P stays the same; Q grows about ten times over
quiz.explain: Printing one name is a fixed amount of work; comparing every pair grows with the square of the count, so ten times the names is a hundred times the work.

quiz.prompt: A sorted list holds 1024 items and a program throws away half of what is left at each step. How many halvings take it down to a single item?
quiz.explain: 1024 halves to 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and finally 1: ten steps.

quiz.prompt: Program A doubles its work when the list doubles. Program B quadruples its work when the list doubles. On a list ten times larger, roughly what happens?
quiz.answer: A does about ten times the work; B does about a hundred times
choices: A does about ten times the work; B does about a hundred times
Both do about ten times the work
A does twice the work and B four times, whatever the list size
B does about twenty times the work
quiz.explain: A grows in step with the list; B grows with the square of it, so a factor of ten becomes a factor of a hundred.

quiz.prompt: A program compares every possible pair of items in a list of 6 items, counting each pair once. How many pairs are there?
quiz.explain: Each of the 6 items pairs with 5 others, and each pair is counted twice, so 6 x 5 / 2 = 15.

quiz.prompt: A phone book is in no particular order. A friend suggests searching it by halving, as binary search does. Why will that fail?
quiz.answer: Halving only works when the order tells you which half to keep
choices: Halving only works when the order tells you which half to keep
Halving is too slow once the book is large
You would need to sort each half again every time
Halving works, but it takes twice as many steps unsorted
quiz.explain: Binary search throws away half the data because order guarantees the target cannot be there. Without order nothing can be ruled out, so the method does not become slower - it stops being correct.

lesson_media.alt: For sixteen sorted cards, linear search checks up to sixteen cards one by one, while binary search halves the remaining interval and needs at most five checks.
lesson_media.caption: Algorithm speed depends on how work grows with input size. Linear search can inspect every item; binary search uses sorted order to discard half the candidates after each comparison.

nodes.title: Data Structures
nodes.goal: Arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables.

lesson_media.alt: Matching blue cube, green sphere, yellow pyramid, red cylinder and purple star blocks sit in a vertical stack and a horizontal queue; arrows show the stack's top star leaving, the queue's front cube leaving and another star entering at the rear.
lesson_media.caption: A stack removes from the top in last-in, first-out order; a queue removes from the front and adds at the rear in first-in, first-out order.

lesson_media.title: Compare a stack and a queue
lesson_media.instructions: Switch between stack and queue mode, then add and remove shape-coded blocks. Watch which end accepts a new block and which block leaves next.

quiz.prompt: A program processes print jobs in the exact order they were submitted: the first job sent is the first one printed. Which data structure models this behavior?
quiz.answer: Queue (FIFO)
quiz.explain: First-in, first-out ordering is exactly what a queue provides.
choices: Stack (LIFO)
Queue (FIFO)
Priority heap
Sorted array

quiz.prompt: You need to check thousands of times whether a given username already exists in a large collection. Assuming a suitable hash function, ordinary constant-time key hashing and equality checks, and a load factor kept bounded by resizing, which structure gives the best expected average lookup time?
quiz.answer: A hash table, with average O(1) lookup
quiz.explain: Under those hashing, key-cost, load-factor and resizing assumptions, a hash table has expected O(1) average lookup; this is not a worst-case guarantee. Sorted arrays and balanced trees are O(log n), while a linear scan is O(n).
choices: A hash table, with average O(1) lookup
A sorted array, with a binary search each time
A balanced search tree, with O(log n) lookup
An unsorted array, scanned from the start each time

quiz.prompt: You push 1, 2, then 3 onto an empty stack, then pop three times. In what order do the values come off?
quiz.explain: A stack is last-in, first-out, so the pops reverse the order the values went in.

quiz.prompt: A perfect binary tree has 4 levels: a root plus three more levels below it, with every level full. How many nodes does it hold altogether?
quiz.explain: Level sizes double: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15, so a perfect binary tree with every one of its h levels full holds 2^h - 1 nodes.

quiz.prompt: A program keeps 10,000 records and constantly inserts new ones at the front of the collection. Which storage keeps each insertion cheap, and why?
quiz.answer: A linked list, since a new head only relinks one pointer
choices: A linked list, since a new head only relinks one pointer
An array, since its items sit side by side in memory
A sorted array, since insertion can use binary search
A hash table, since it stores items without any order
quiz.explain: Inserting at the front of an array shifts every later element, costing O(n); a linked list just points the new node at the old head, costing O(1).

quiz.prompt: Two different keys hash to the same bucket in a separately chained hash table. What does a correct implementation do?
quiz.answer: Store both in that bucket and compare keys on lookup
choices: Store both in that bucket and compare keys on lookup
Overwrite the first key's value with the second one
Refuse the second key and report the table as full
Rebuild the whole table with a different hash function
quiz.explain: With separate chaining, collisions are expected: the bucket holds both entries in a chain and lookup compares their full keys, so distinct keys are not confused. Open-addressed tables resolve collisions differently by probing other slots.

quiz.prompt: A queue receives A, B, C and D in that order. Two items are then dequeued and E is enqueued. How many items are in the queue?
quiz.explain: Four in, two out, one in: 4 - 2 + 1 = 3 items remain.

quiz.prompt: The values 5, 3 and 8 are pushed onto an empty stack in that order, one item is popped, and then the value 2 is pushed. What does the stack hold, read from top to bottom?
quiz.explain: The pop removes 8, the most recent push, leaving 3 above 5; pushing 2 places it on top.

quiz.prompt: A program must read the 5,000th element of a fixed 10,000-element collection millions of times and never inserts anything. Which storage suits it, and why?
quiz.answer: An array, since an index computes the address directly
choices: An array, since an index computes the address directly
A linked list, since its pointers skip ahead quickly
A stack, since the top is reached instantly
A queue, since the order of elements is preserved
quiz.explain: Array elements sit contiguously, so element k is found by arithmetic. A linked list must walk 5,000 links each time.

quiz.prompt: A separately chained hash table has expected constant-time lookup when keys spread well, but a badly chosen hash function sends every key to the same bucket. Explain why lookup can then take time proportional to the number of keys.
quiz.answer: All the entries end up on one bucket's chain, so a lookup can no longer jump straight to a short bucket and must instead scan that single chain linearly through every stored key.
quiz.explain: Expected constant-time lookup in a separately chained table depends on keys spreading well and the load factor staying bounded so bucket chains remain short.

nodes.title: Algorithms
nodes.goal: Searching, sorting, recursion and complexity.

quiz.prompt: Binary search requires its input to have a specific property. Which is it?
quiz.answer: The data must be sorted
quiz.explain: Binary search relies on order to decide which half to discard. Duplicates are fine, any ordered type works including text, and a linked list is in fact the wrong shape because it cannot jump to the middle.
choices: The data must be free of repeated values
The data must be stored in a linked list
The data must be numbers rather than text
The data must be sorted

quiz.prompt:
Consider this recursive function:

  factorial(n):
    if n == 0: return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

What does factorial(4) return?
Algorithm X sorts n items in about n² comparisons; algorithm Y sorts them in about n·log(n) comparisons. As the list grows very large, what happens?
quiz.answer: Y increasingly outperforms X as the list grows large
quiz.explain: n·log(n) grows much more slowly than n², so Y's advantage increases with larger inputs.
choices: Y is faster just for lists shorter than 10 items
Y increasingly outperforms X as the list grows large
They stay roughly equal since both sort correctly
X becomes faster because n² grows more slowly for big n

quiz.prompt: Binary search runs on a sorted array of 1,000 items and each comparison halves the range that is left. How many comparisons does the worst case need?
quiz.explain: Ten halvings cut 1,000 down to a single item, since 2^10 = 1024, so the worst case is about log2(1000) = 10 comparisons.

quiz.prompt:
A student writes

  countdown(n):
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)

and calls countdown(5). What happens when it runs?
quiz.answer: It prints numbers past zero until the call stack runs out of room
choices: It prints numbers past zero until the call stack runs out of room
It prints 5 down to 1 and then returns quietly
It prints 5 once and stops, since n has changed
It refuses to compile, because a function may not call itself
quiz.explain: Recursion needs a base case. Without a test such as 'if n < 0: return', the calls keep going and the stack fills up.

quiz.prompt: A list of 1,000,000 integers is already almost sorted: fewer than 20 items sit out of place. Which sort finishes fastest on it?
quiz.answer: Insertion sort, which is nearly linear on almost-sorted input
choices: Insertion sort, which is nearly linear on almost-sorted input
Selection sort, which scans the remaining items each round
Bubble sort with fixed passes and no early exit
Merge sort, which splits and merges whatever the order
quiz.explain: Insertion sort costs about n plus the number of items out of place, so nearly sorted input is close to one pass; merge sort still pays n log n.

quiz.prompt: Merge sort splits a list of 8 items in half repeatedly until every piece holds one item. How many levels of splitting does that take?
quiz.explain: 8 splits to 4, then 2, then 1: three levels, which is log base 2 of 8.

quiz.prompt:
A recursive function is defined as:

  fib(n):
    if n <= 1: return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

What does fib(6) return?
quiz.explain: The sequence runs 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so fib(6) is 8.

quiz.prompt: Selection sort scans the unsorted part for the smallest item on every pass. How much work does it do on a list of 1,000 items that is already sorted?
quiz.answer: About the same as on a random list
choices: About the same as on a random list
Far less, because it stops as soon as the list is sorted
Twice as much, because no swaps are needed
None, because sorted input is detected before it starts
quiz.explain: Since it scans regardless. Selection sort has no early exit: it always searches the remaining part for a minimum, so sorted input saves nothing.

quiz.prompt: One pass of bubble sort, comparing neighbours from left to right and swapping any that are out of order, is applied to [4, 1, 3, 2]. What does the list look like after that single pass?
quiz.explain: 4 swaps past 1, then past 3, then past 2, carrying the largest value to the end; the rest shift left by one.

lesson_media.alt: Merge sort transforms 7 2 5 1 by recursively splitting it into two pairs, ordering each pair, and merging 2 7 with 1 5 to produce 1 2 5 7.
lesson_media.caption: Merge sort uses divide, recurse, and combine. Each merge is linear in the items merged; across logarithmically many split levels, total time grows on the order of n log n.

nodes.title: Object-Oriented Programming
nodes.goal: Classes, objects, inheritance.

quiz.prompt: A class Dog inherits from a class Animal. Animal defines a method speak(). Dog overrides speak() to return "Woof". If you call speak() on a Dog object, what happens?
quiz.answer: Dog's version runs, returning "Woof"
quiz.explain: An overriding method in the subclass takes precedence for instances of that subclass.
choices: Animal's version runs, since it was defined first
Both versions run and their results are combined
It is an error to override an inherited method
Dog's version runs, returning "Woof"

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a class and an object?
quiz.answer: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance made from it
quiz.explain: The class defines structure and behavior; each object is a concrete instance with its own data.
choices: A class and an object are two names for the very same thing
A class stores the data while an object stores the methods
A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance made from it
An object is the blueprint; a class is an instance made from it

quiz.prompt: You are modeling shapes. Circle, Square, and Triangle each need their own area() calculation but share a common type. Which OOP design best captures this?
quiz.answer: A base class Shape with an area() method that each subclass overrides
quiz.explain: Inheritance with an overridden method lets each shape share a type while defining its own area. A kind field with a switch inside area() gets the shared type but puts every formula back in one place that must be edited for each new shape.
choices: One giant function with a long chain of if-statements and no classes
A Shape class holding a kind field that area() switches on
Three unrelated classes with no shared parent and duplicated code
A base class Shape with an area() method that each subclass overrides

quiz.prompt: A Rectangle class keeps width and height as private fields and offers getArea() and setWidth(). The team later rewrites it to store two corner coordinates instead. Why did keeping the fields private make that rewrite safe?
quiz.answer: Outside code could only reach the rectangle through its methods, so the private fields were free to change without breaking a single caller.
quiz.explain: Encapsulation fixes a public interface and hides the representation, so the class can be reimplemented as long as the methods keep their meaning.

quiz.prompt: A designer makes Car inherit from Engine so that a Car can call start(). What is wrong with that design?
quiz.answer: A car has an engine rather than being one, so a field fits better
choices: A car has an engine rather than being one, so a field fits better
Inheritance is slower at run time than storing a field
A class may inherit from just one parent in most languages
Engine should inherit from Car so that start is shared
quiz.explain: Inheritance models 'is-a'. An engine is a part, so Car should hold an Engine field and pass start() along to it - composition, not inheritance.

quiz.prompt: Shape defines draw(). Circle and Square each override it. A list declared as Shape holds one Circle and one Square, and a loop calls draw() on each. Which code runs?
quiz.answer: Each object's own override, chosen at run time by its class
choices: Each object's own override, chosen at run time by its class
Shape's draw() both times, since the list is declared as Shape
Circle's draw() both times, since it comes first in the list
Neither: a list may not mix two different subclasses
quiz.explain: Dynamic dispatch chooses the method from the object's actual class, not from the type of the variable or list that holds it.

quiz.prompt: A class Point stores x and y. A program creates p = Point(1, 2) and q = Point(1, 2). What is true of p and q?
quiz.answer: They are separate objects that happen to hold equal values
choices: They are separate objects that happen to hold equal values
They are the same object, since their values match
Changing p.x will also change q.x
p == q is true, since the constructor was given the same values
quiz.explain: Each call to the constructor builds a new object with its own fields, so writing to one leaves the other alone. Whether p == q holds depends on whether the class defines equality by value; by default it compares identity and is false.

quiz.prompt: A BankAccount class exposes balance as a public field, and a bug elsewhere sets it to a negative number. Which change prevents that whole class of bug?
quiz.answer: Make balance private and change it only through deposit and withdraw
choices: Make balance private and change it only through deposit and withdraw
Add a comment warning other programmers not to set balance directly
Rename the field to _balance to signal that it is internal
Add a check in every place that currently assigns to balance
quiz.explain: Encapsulation puts the rule in one place the compiler enforces. A comment, a naming convention and a check repeated at each call site all depend on every future author remembering; the next assignment added elsewhere skips all three.

quiz.prompt: A class Counter declares one instance field. A program creates ten Counter objects. How many separate copies of that field exist?
quiz.explain: An instance field belongs to the object, so each of the ten objects carries its own copy.

quiz.prompt: Animal defines speak() returning 'generic'. Cat extends Animal and overrides speak(); Dog extends Animal and does not. A loop calls speak() on one Cat and one Dog. What comes back?
quiz.answer: The Cat's own version, then 'generic' inherited from Animal
choices: The Cat's own version, then 'generic' inherited from Animal
'generic' twice, since the loop variable is declared as Animal
The Cat's version twice, since it is the more specific one
An error, because Dog defines no speak()
quiz.explain: A subclass that does not override a method inherits it, and the version that runs is chosen by the object's real class.

lesson_media.alt: A Vehicle class containing speed and move branches to Bike and Car subclasses; two bike objects then hold different speed values despite sharing behavior.
lesson_media.caption: A class defines fields and behavior, while each object has its own state. Inheritance can share an interface or implementation, but composition is often preferable when the relation is not truly is-a.

nodes.title: Building for the Web
nodes.goal: HTML, CSS and JavaScript make interactive pages.

quiz.prompt: On a web page, which technology is responsible for the structure and content (headings, paragraphs, buttons), as opposed to appearance or behavior?
quiz.answer: HTML
quiz.explain: HTML defines the structure and content; CSS handles styling and JavaScript handles behavior.
choices: JavaScript
HTML
CSS
SQL

quiz.prompt: A designer wants every button on the site to have a blue background and rounded corners, without touching the page's content or logic. Which technology should they use?
quiz.answer: CSS
quiz.explain: CSS controls presentation such as colors and shapes, separate from content (HTML) and behavior (JavaScript).
choices: HTTP
CSS
HTML
JavaScript

quiz.prompt: When a user clicks a button and the page instantly updates a counter without reloading, which technology is most directly responsible?
quiz.answer: JavaScript, which adds behavior in the browser
quiz.explain: JavaScript runs in the browser to respond to events and update the page dynamically.
choices: JavaScript, which adds behavior in the browser
CSS, which styles the counter's appearance
HTML, which lists the page's static content
SQL, which stores the counter inside a database

quiz.prompt: A page asks the server for 1 HTML file, 3 CSS files, 5 images and 2 scripts, each as its own HTTP request. How many requests does the browser make in total?
quiz.explain: Every linked resource is a separate request: 1 + 3 + 5 + 2 = 11, which is why bundling files makes pages load faster.

quiz.prompt: A shopping page hides its 'admin' button from ordinary users with CSS. A visitor opens the browser's developer tools and unhides it. What does that show?
quiz.answer: Checks that matter belong on the server, since the browser obeys the user
choices: Checks that matter belong on the server, since the browser obeys the user
The button should be removed from the HTML instead of hidden
The page should hide the button with JavaScript rather than CSS
The admin check should run when the page is first built
quiz.explain: Anything sent to the browser can be read and changed by whoever holds it. Leaving the button out of the HTML hides the control but not the endpoint it calls, and a check made while building the page is still a decision the server must repeat when the request arrives.

quiz.prompt: A form submits and the browser gets back status code 404. What went wrong?
quiz.answer: The server could not find the address the form posted to
choices: The browser blocked the request for security reasons
The server could not find the address the form posted to
The user's internet connection dropped during the request
The server took the data but has not finished saving it
quiz.explain: 404 is the server's own reply saying the requested path does not exist, so the request arrived fine but pointed nowhere.

quiz.prompt: A page's HTML arrives but its CSS file fails to load. What does the visitor see?
quiz.answer: The content, unstyled
choices: The content, unstyled
A completely blank page
An error message instead
The styling but no text
quiz.explain: HTML carries the content; CSS only decorates it, so losing the stylesheet leaves plain but readable content.

quiz.prompt: A CSS rule gives a box a width of 200px, padding of 10px on each side and a 5px border on each side. Under the default content-box sizing, how many pixels wide does it occupy on screen?
quiz.explain: Content-box sizing adds padding and border outside the stated width: 200 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 230.

quiz.prompt: A form lets a user set a new password. Which HTTP method should carry the submission, and why?
quiz.answer: POST, because it sends the data in the request body rather than in the visible URL
choices: POST, because it sends the data in the request body rather than in the visible URL
GET, because the browser handles it faster
GET, because the result can then be bookmarked
Either one, since both conceal the data equally
quiz.explain: A GET puts the values in the URL, where they land in history, logs and referrer headers.

quiz.prompt: A script placed in the page's head tries to change an element defined further down the page and fails with 'element not found'. Explain the cause and one fix.
quiz.answer: The script runs while the browser is still parsing the HTML below it, so the element is not yet in the DOM; move the script to the end of the body or mark it defer so it waits until the document has finished loading.
quiz.explain: Scripts execute at the point they appear unless deferred, and they can only see the document built so far.

lesson_media.alt: A web button is built in layers: HTML supplies the button element, CSS sets its visible style, JavaScript handles a click, and the browser combines them into interactive output.
lesson_media.caption: HTML describes document structure, CSS applies presentation, and JavaScript can update state and behavior. The browser parses and combines these resources into an accessible interface.

nodes.title: Databases
nodes.goal: Store and query data with SQL.

quiz.prompt: A table Users has columns id, name, and age. Which SQL query returns the names of users older than 30?
quiz.answer: SELECT name FROM Users WHERE age > 30
quiz.explain: SELECT chooses the column (name) and WHERE filters the rows (age > 30).
choices: SELECT * FROM Users ORDER BY age DESC
SELECT name FROM Users WHERE age > 30
FIND name FROM Users WHERE age > 30
SELECT age FROM Users WHERE name > '30'

quiz.prompt: In a relational database, an Orders table stores a customer_id that refers to the id of a row in the Customers table. What is customer_id called here?
quiz.answer: A foreign key
quiz.explain: A foreign key is a column that references the primary key of another table, linking the two.
choices: A foreign key
A composite key
A lookup index
A primary key

quiz.prompt: Why is storing each customer's details once in a Customers table (and referencing them by id elsewhere) better than repeating those details in every Orders row?
quiz.answer: It avoids duplication, so an update happens in one place
quiz.explain: Normalization stores facts once, preventing inconsistent duplicates when data changes. A foreign key can also enforce that the referenced customer exists, but that is the constraint's doing rather than the reason for splitting the tables.
choices: It keeps the Orders table small enough to fit in memory
It makes queries run at a fixed speed whatever the table size
It avoids duplication, so an update happens in one place
It lets the database check that each customer really exists

quiz.prompt: Table A holds 5 rows and table B holds 3 rows. A query joins them with no join condition at all. How many rows does the result contain?
quiz.explain: Without a condition the join pairs every row of A with every row of B: 5 x 3 = 15. A forgotten ON clause produces exactly this blow-up.

quiz.prompt: An Orders table has columns customer_id and amount. Which query gives the total amount spent by each customer?
quiz.answer: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id
choices: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM Orders
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM Orders ORDER BY customer_id
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM Orders WHERE customer_id > 0
quiz.explain: GROUP BY splits the rows into one group per customer and SUM adds within each group; without it the aggregate collapses the whole table to one number.

quiz.prompt: A Students table uses the surname as its primary key. The school enrols a second student with the same surname. What happens, and what should change?
quiz.answer: The insert is rejected; a unique id column should be the key
choices: The insert is rejected; a unique id column should be the key
Both rows are stored, and the older one becomes hidden
The insert succeeds, since surnames are only usually unique
The second row overwrites the first, since the keys match
quiz.explain: A primary key has to be unique, so the duplicate is refused outright - it is not hidden, merged or overwritten. A surrogate id avoids depending on real-world data staying unique.

quiz.prompt: A query reads  SELECT name FROM Users ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 3. What does it return?
quiz.answer: The names of the three oldest users
choices: The names of the three oldest users
The names of the three youngest users
Three names in alphabetical order
The names of users older than three
quiz.explain: ORDER BY age DESC puts the largest ages first, and LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows of that ordering.

quiz.prompt: Customers holds 8 rows. Orders holds 20 rows, each referencing a customer that exists. An INNER JOIN of Orders to Customers on customer_id returns how many rows?
quiz.explain: Each order matches exactly one customer, so every order contributes one row and no order is dropped.

quiz.prompt: After joining Orders to Customers, a report shows each customer's name several times. Why?
quiz.answer: A customer with several orders appears once per order
choices: A customer with several orders appears once per order
The join lost the Customers primary key
An INNER JOIN always duplicates rows
The Customers table stores each customer more than once
quiz.explain: A join produces one row per matching pair, so a one-to-many relationship repeats the 'one' side.

quiz.prompt: A column phone allows NULL. The query  WHERE phone != '0000'  leaves out the rows whose phone is NULL. Why?
quiz.answer: Comparing anything with NULL yields unknown, not true
choices: Comparing anything with NULL yields unknown, not true
NULL counts as the empty string, which matches '0000'
The query contains a syntax error
Rows with NULL are kept in a separate part of the table
quiz.explain: SQL uses three-valued logic. Only rows where the condition is definitely true are returned, so IS NULL must be asked for explicitly.

lesson_media.alt: A four-row books table is filtered by the SQL condition year at least 2020 and rating above 4, producing only the two rows that satisfy both predicates.
lesson_media.caption: A relational query transforms a table into a result relation. WHERE keeps rows for which the complete Boolean condition is true; it does not modify the stored table.

nodes.title: How Computers Work
nodes.goal: Logic gates, memory and the CPU.

quiz.prompt: The same two signals, A = 1 and B = 0, are fed to an AND gate and to an OR gate. What does each gate output?
quiz.answer: AND gives 0, OR gives 1
choices: AND gives 1, OR gives 1
AND gives 0, OR gives 1
AND gives 1, OR gives 0
AND gives 0, OR gives 0
quiz.explain: AND needs both inputs high, so it outputs 0; OR needs just one, so it outputs 1.

quiz.prompt: Using Boolean algebra, the expression NOT (A AND B) is equivalent to which of the following?
quiz.answer: (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
quiz.explain: By De Morgan's law, the negation of an AND becomes an OR of the negations.
choices: A AND B
(NOT A) AND (NOT B)
(NOT A) OR (NOT B)
A OR B

quiz.prompt: In the fetch-decode-execute cycle, what does the CPU do in the 'fetch' step?
quiz.answer: Retrieve the next instruction from memory
quiz.explain: Fetch loads the next instruction from memory; decode interprets it and execute carries it out.
choices: Retrieve the next instruction from memory
Translate the program from a high-level language
Write the final result back to disk
Perform the arithmetic for the instruction

quiz.prompt: What is the decimal value of the 8-bit binary number 00101101?
quiz.explain: Reading from the right, the set bits are worth 1, 4, 8 and 32, and 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

quiz.prompt: A CPU finishes an instruction in under a nanosecond, but a read from main memory takes about 60 nanoseconds. Which design decision follows from that gap?
quiz.answer: Keep recently used data in a small fast cache beside the core
choices: Keep recently used data in a small fast cache beside the core
Raise the clock speed so instructions finish sooner
Move the program's data onto the hard drive instead
Give each instruction its own copy of main memory
quiz.explain: Caches exploit locality: keeping hot data next to the core hides most of the memory delay, which a faster clock alone cannot do.

quiz.prompt: A half adder produces a sum output of A XOR B and a carry output of A AND B. Feed it A = 1 and B = 1. What does it produce?
quiz.answer: Sum 0, carry 1
choices: Sum 0, carry 1
Sum 1, carry 0
Sum 1, carry 1
Sum 0, carry 0
quiz.explain: 1 XOR 1 is 0 and 1 AND 1 is 1, so 1 + 1 in binary is 10: a sum bit of 0 with a carry of 1.

quiz.prompt: What is the decimal value of the 8-bit binary number 10110000?
quiz.explain: The set bits carry 128, 32 and 16, and 128 + 32 + 16 = 176.

quiz.prompt: A circuit must pass a signal B through unchanged when a control line A is 0, and flip B when A is 1. Which single gate does that?
quiz.answer: XOR
choices: AND
OR
XOR
NAND
quiz.explain: XOR outputs 1 exactly when its inputs differ, so 0 XOR B is B and 1 XOR B is the inverse of B.

quiz.prompt: Power is cut in the middle of editing. The unsaved text is gone but the last saved file survives. Which difference explains that?
quiz.answer: RAM loses its contents without power, while the drive keeps them
choices: RAM loses its contents without power, while the drive keeps them
RAM is smaller than the drive, so the text overflowed
The editor had not yet been given the text to store
The drive is faster, so it finished writing before the power went
quiz.explain: RAM is volatile working memory; a drive is non-volatile storage, which is exactly why saving matters. The editor did hold the text, and it is permanence rather than speed or capacity that separates the two.

quiz.prompt: Two CPUs run at the same clock speed, yet one finishes the same program in half the time. Which explanation is plausible?
quiz.answer: It completes more instructions per clock cycle
choices: It completes more instructions per clock cycle
Its clock ticks last longer, so more happens in each
It runs at a higher voltage, which raises the clock
It has more cores, though the program uses only one
quiz.explain: Clock speed counts ticks per second; how much useful work happens per tick depends on pipelining, width and cache. Extra cores do nothing for a single-threaded program, and a tick's length is what the clock speed already states.

lesson_media.alt: Two logic panels derive a one-bit half adder: XOR produces the sum bit and AND produces the carry bit, with input 1 and 1 yielding sum 0 and carry 1.
lesson_media.caption: Logic gates implement Boolean functions in hardware. For two one-bit inputs, XOR records whether exactly one input is one, while AND records the carry when both are one.

nodes.title: Tools of the Trade
nodes.goal: Version control, testing and working in teams.

quiz.prompt: Two teammates edit the same file on separate Git branches and both change the same line differently. When merging, what happens?
quiz.answer: Git reports a merge conflict that a human must resolve
