quiz.explain: When the same line diverges, Git cannot decide automatically and flags a conflict. It does mark up the file with both versions, but as a conflict to be resolved rather than as two lines to keep, and commit timestamps never decide the winner.
choices: Git takes whichever change was committed most recently
Git silently keeps the older change
Git reports a merge conflict that a human must resolve
Git keeps both lines, one after the other, in the file

quiz.prompt: You made several commits today and realize a change from this morning broke the app. How does version control most directly help?
quiz.answer: It keeps a commit history you can inspect and revert to
quiz.explain: Version control records a history you can diff and roll back to. Blame tells you who, not what broke; nothing in Git knows which state ran; and refusing broken commits is a hook or a CI system layered on top, not the tool itself.
choices: It keeps a commit history you can inspect and revert to
It prevents anyone from committing code that fails to build
It restores the working directory to the last state that ran
It records which teammate last edited each broken line

quiz.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an automated test suite in a team codebase?
quiz.answer: To catch regressions automatically before release
quiz.explain: Tests verify behavior automatically, flagging when a change breaks something that previously worked. A good suite does document usage as a side effect, but that is a benefit rather than the purpose, and passing tests never prove the absence of bugs.
choices: To make the finished program run faster in production
To catch regressions automatically before release
To guarantee the code has zero bugs of any kind
To describe how the code should be used by new joiners

quiz.prompt: Your team works on one shared branch and everyone commits straight to it. Give one concrete problem this causes that feature branches with pull requests would avoid.
quiz.answer: Half-finished work lands straight on the shared branch, where it can break the build for everyone, and nothing forces a review before the change merges.
quiz.explain: Feature branches keep work in progress out of the shared line and give reviewers a checkpoint, so the main branch stays buildable.

quiz.prompt: A test passed 200 commits ago and fails now. Checking any one commit takes 5 minutes. Which approach finds the breaking commit fastest?
quiz.answer: Binary search the history, about 8 checks
choices: Binary search the history, about 8 checks
Check all 200 commits oldest to newest
Check the 10 most recent commits and guess from there
Revert the whole range and reapply the commits one by one
quiz.explain: Bisecting halves the suspect range each time, so log2(200) is about 8 checks - 40 minutes rather than most of a day.

quiz.prompt: You committed a file holding your API password, then made 3 more commits. Deleting the file in a new commit is not enough. Why not?
quiz.answer: The password stays readable in the earlier commit in history
choices: The password stays readable in the earlier commit in history
The delete commit has to be pushed before it takes effect
The file returns whenever the branch is merged elsewhere
Git keeps deleted files until the repository is packed
quiz.explain: History is append-only, so every earlier commit still contains the file and anyone with the repository can check it out. The secret has to be rotated and the history rewritten or purged.

quiz.prompt: You edit three files, run  git add  on two of them, then commit. What lands in the commit?
quiz.answer: Only the two files that were staged
choices: Only the two files that were staged
All three edited files in the working directory
Nothing, because the commit is refused
All three, with the unstaged one marked as partial
quiz.explain: The staging area is what a commit records; unstaged edits stay in the working directory for a later commit.

quiz.prompt: Two branches change completely different files and are then merged. What happens?
quiz.answer: Git merges them automatically with no conflict
choices: Git merges them automatically with no conflict
Git reports a conflict for every file that changed
Git merges only if the branches share their latest commit
Git keeps the newer branch's files and drops the other's
quiz.explain: A conflict arises only when the same region of the same file was changed in both branches. Branches are expected to have diverged - that is what merging is for - and neither side's files are dropped.

quiz.prompt: A team runs 400 automated tests one after another and each takes 3 seconds. How many minutes does a complete run take?
quiz.explain: 400 x 3 = 1,200 seconds, and 1,200 divided by 60 is 20 minutes.

quiz.prompt: Why should a commit message explain why a change was made rather than restate which lines changed?
quiz.answer: The diff already shows which lines changed, so repeating it adds nothing; what the code cannot record is why the change was needed, and knowing why is what lets a future reader judge whether the change is still correct.
quiz.explain: History is read months later by someone tracking down a bug, and the reason behind a change is the part that cannot be recovered from the code.

lesson_media.alt: A main commit splits into feature and bug-fix branches, each passes tests, and both changes join through reviewed merge commits while preserving history.
lesson_media.caption: Version control records a graph of changes rather than one mutable file. Branches isolate work; automated tests and review provide evidence before integration, though they cannot prove absence of every bug.

nodes.title: Advanced Algorithms
nodes.goal: Dynamic programming, graphs, greedy methods.

quiz.prompt: A naive recursive fib(n) takes exponential time. Storing each fib(k) in a table the first time it is computed brings the running time down to about n steps. Which property of the problem is what makes the table pay off?
quiz.answer: Different branches ask for the same subproblems
quiz.explain: The exponential cost comes from re-solving overlapping subproblems, not from depth and not from the cost of a single call: fib(n) is n deep either way. The table pays because fib(k) is asked for many times, so the second and later requests are free.
choices: Different branches ask for the same subproblems
The recursion tree is deep, and the table shortens its depth
Each recursive call becomes one table lookup instead of one addition
Recursion is slow, and the table replaces it with a loop

quiz.prompt: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step. For which problem does a greedy strategy NOT always yield the optimal answer?
quiz.answer: Making change with arbitrary coin denominations
quiz.explain: With arbitrary denominations, greedy can fail (e.g., coins 1,3,4 making 6), unlike the other problems where greedy is provably optimal.
choices: Finding a minimum spanning tree (Kruskal's algorithm)
Building an optimal prefix code (Huffman coding)
Making change with arbitrary coin denominations
Selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping activities

quiz.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm settles vertices in nondecreasing order of their final distance from the source and never revisits a settled vertex. A driver needs the distance to one particular target, not to all of them. What does that ordering let the implementation do?
quiz.answer: Stop as soon as the target is settled
quiz.explain: The settling order is the guarantee: when a vertex leaves the queue its distance is already final, so the search can stop there. A tentative distance may still fall, nothing licenses processing vertices in input order, and the target's distance is unknown until it settles, so it cannot be used to skip work beforehand.
choices: Stop as soon as the target is settled
Read the target's tentative distance before it is settled
Process the vertices in the order they were listed
Skip every vertex farther away than the target

quiz.prompt: The standard dynamic-programming table for edit distance fills one cell per pair of prefixes, counting the empty prefix of each string. For strings of length 9 and 12, how many cells does the table hold?
quiz.explain: The table measures (m+1) by (n+1) because both empty prefixes get a row and a column: 10 x 13 = 130 cells, each filled in constant time.

quiz.prompt: A routing service runs Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph where some edges carry negative weights to represent refunds. Several paths come out wrong. Which change fixes it?
quiz.answer: Use Bellman-Ford, which copes with negative edges
choices: Use Bellman-Ford, which copes with negative edges
Add a large constant to every edge weight before running Dijkstra
Run Dijkstra from each vertex and keep the shortest result
Sort the edges by weight and process the negative ones first
quiz.explain: Dijkstra assumes a settled vertex can never improve, which negative edges break. Adding a constant penalises paths with more edges, changing which path wins.

quiz.prompt: Coins come in denominations 1, 7 and 10. A greedy cashier repeatedly hands over the largest coin that still fits, making 15. How many coins does greedy use, and how many does the best answer use?
quiz.answer: Greedy uses 6 coins; the best answer uses 3
choices: Greedy uses 6 coins; the best answer uses 3
Greedy uses 6 coins, which is already the best
Greedy uses 3 coins; the best answer uses 2
Greedy uses 2 coins; the best answer uses 6
quiz.explain: Greedy takes 10 and then five 1s, six coins in all, while 7 + 7 + 1 needs three. Greedy change-making is optimal only for canonical coin systems.

quiz.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap costs about E log V operations. A road graph has V = 1,000 and E = 5,000, and log base 2 of 1,000 is taken as 10. Give the resulting number of operations.
quiz.explain: 5,000 edges times 10 gives 50,000 heap operations.

quiz.prompt: A scheduler must choose jobs with given values and durations to fill exactly 60 minutes, and taking the highest-value job first misses the best combination. Which method returns the optimum in time proportional to jobs times minutes?
quiz.answer: Fill a table indexed by job and remaining minutes
choices: Fill a table indexed by job and remaining minutes
Sort jobs by value per minute and take greedily until the time is used up
Enumerate every subset of jobs and keep the best
Swap random pairs of jobs until no swap improves the total
quiz.explain: This is a knapsack over time. The table is the dynamic-programming solution; enumeration is exponential and the other two are heuristics.

quiz.prompt: A build system with 200 tasks and dependencies between them reports that no task is ready to start. What has happened, and what detects it?
quiz.answer: A dependency cycle, which a topological sort cannot order
choices: A dependency cycle, which a topological sort cannot order
A prerequisite that no task defines, leaving everything blocked
Every task marked as depending on another, with none seeded
More dependency edges than there are tasks to schedule
quiz.explain: A topological order exists exactly for acyclic graphs, so 'nothing is ready' with every task holding an unmet prerequisite is the signature of a cycle. An undefined prerequisite blocks its dependents but not the tasks that have none, edge count says nothing about readiness, and a task with no prerequisites at all is what seeds the sort.

quiz.prompt: A campus must join 12 buildings with fibre at the least total cost, and any loop of cable is wasted. Which algorithm applies?
quiz.answer: Kruskal's, adding the cheapest edges that do not close a cycle
choices: Kruskal's, adding the cheapest edges that do not close a cycle
Dijkstra's, growing shortest paths outward from the main building
Depth-first search from the main building, keeping the edges it uses
Bellman-Ford, relaxing all edges for every pair of buildings
quiz.explain: This is a minimum spanning tree, not a shortest-path problem: cheapest total cable, not cheapest route between any pair.

lesson_media.alt: A weighted graph sends paths from S through A or B to T; edge weights show S-A-T costs 7, S-B-T costs 6, and relaxation selects the lower distance six.
lesson_media.caption: Shortest-path algorithms maintain tentative distances and relax an edge when it gives a cheaper route. With nonnegative weights, Dijkstra's greedy finalization is correct under its stated invariant.

nodes.title: Theory of Computation
nodes.goal: Automata, Turing machines, and the limits of computing.

quiz.prompt: The halting problem asks whether a given program halts on a given input. What did Turing prove about it?
quiz.answer: No algorithm decides it for all program-input pairs
quiz.explain: Turing's result is about decidability, not speed: no program at all, however slow, decides halting for every input. Running the candidate is a semi-decision procedure - it says yes when the program halts but never says no - and the limit is mathematical, so no hardware removes it.
choices: No algorithm decides it for all program-input pairs
It becomes solvable once quantum computers are built
It can be decided by running the program on that input
It is decidable, but no efficient method is known

quiz.prompt: Two DFAs, one with 4 states and one with 6, accept languages L1 and L2. The product construction builds a DFA for L1 intersect L2 by running both machines at once. At most how many states does the result need, and why?
quiz.answer: 24, one for each pair of states
quiz.explain: The product machine has to remember where each original machine is, so its states are the pairs: 4 x 6 = 24. Pooling the states would lose track of one machine, and the exponential blow-up belongs to determinising an NFA, not to intersecting two DFAs.
choices: 24, one for each pair of states
10, since the two state sets are pooled
6, since the larger machine dominates
1024, since subsets of the combined states are needed

quiz.prompt: Why is a Turing machine, despite its simplicity, central to the theory of computation?
quiz.answer: It captures everything that is effectively computable
quiz.explain: The Church-Turing thesis says the Turing-computable functions are exactly the effectively computable ones, and every richer model proposed since - lambda calculus, register machines, quantum circuits - computes the same set. It is a claim about what, not about how fast, and its tape resembles no real CPU.
choices: It captures everything that is effectively computable
It is an accurate model of how a real CPU is built
It marks the boundary of what can be computed quickly
A richer machine model would compute strictly more

quiz.prompt: A DFA over the alphabet {a, b} must accept exactly those strings whose length divides evenly by 4. How many states does the smallest such DFA need?
quiz.explain: Tracking length modulo 4 takes one state per remainder, with the remainder-0 state accepting; three states cannot distinguish four remainders.

quiz.prompt: A student claims a finite automaton can recognise the strings a^n b^n, meaning equally many a's followed by that many b's. Which argument refutes the claim?
quiz.answer: Some two prefixes a^i and a^j share a state, so a^i b^j is accepted too
choices: Some two prefixes a^i and a^j share a state, so a^i b^j is accepted too
The language is infinite, and automata accept only finite sets
Nondeterminism is needed, and a DFA cannot be nondeterministic
Automata read strictly left to right, so they cannot go back and recount the a's
quiz.explain: By the pigeonhole principle a fixed number of states cannot count without bound: two different prefixes collide, and from there the machine cannot tell the counts apart. Plenty of regular languages are infinite, an NFA for this language would fail too, and one-way reading is not the obstacle.

quiz.prompt: You are asked to write a tool that reports whether an arbitrary program ever prints the word ERROR. Why can no such tool be correct on every input?
quiz.answer: Halting reduces to it: make a program print ERROR when it stops
choices: Halting reduces to it: make a program print ERROR when it stops
The tool would have to run the program, which may never stop
A program might print ERROR in a different case or spelling
Rice's theorem covers semantic properties, and printing is syntactic
quiz.explain: Wrap any program P so that it prints ERROR exactly when P stops; a tool answering the printing question would then answer the halting question. 'It might not stop' is the right intuition but rules out one method rather than all of them, spelling is a detail of the wording, and whether a program ever prints a given word is a property of its behaviour, so Rice's theorem does apply — it says every non-trivial property of what a program's behavior actually DOES (as opposed to a property of its source code text) is undecidable, and this reduction from the halting problem is exactly how such undecidability proofs work in practice.

quiz.prompt: A validation tool built from regular expressions must accept parentheses nested to any depth, and it keeps failing on deeply nested input. What does theory say about the attempt?
quiz.answer: Unbounded nesting needs a counter, which a finite automaton lacks
choices: Unbounded nesting needs a counter, which a finite automaton lacks
The engine hit its backtracking limit, which should be raised
Balanced nesting is regular, so the expression is simply mis-written
No language containing unbounded strings can be regular
quiz.explain: A finite automaton has finitely many states, so it cannot remember how many brackets are still open; balanced parentheses is context-free, not regular. Plenty of regular languages contain arbitrarily long strings - a* is one - so length alone is not the obstacle.

quiz.prompt: A DFA over the alphabet {a, b} must accept exactly the strings that end in ab. How many states does the smallest such DFA need?
quiz.explain: One state for 'no useful suffix', one for 'just saw an a' and one accepting state for 'just saw ab'.

quiz.prompt: You produce a polynomial-time construction showing that if problem A could be decided, the halting problem could be decided too. What does that establish about A?
quiz.answer: A is undecidable as well
choices: A is undecidable as well
A is decidable, since halting reduces to it
A belongs to NP
A is decidable only when the inputs are finite
quiz.explain: Reducing an undecidable problem to A means A cannot be easier: a decider for A would give a decider for halting.

quiz.prompt: An NFA with 5 states is turned into an equivalent DFA by the subset construction. What is the largest number of states the DFA might have?
quiz.explain: The construction makes one DFA state per subset of NFA states, and 5 states have 2^5 = 32 subsets.

lesson_media.alt: A three-state deterministic finite automaton tracks whether a binary string currently ends in 01; the accepting double-circle state is reached by input 1101.
lesson_media.caption: A finite automaton remembers only its current state. This DFA recognizes exactly the binary strings ending in 01; other computational models have different power, and some problems are undecidable by any algorithm.

nodes.title: Operating Systems
nodes.goal: Processes, memory, files and concurrency.

quiz.prompt: Two threads both run count = count + 1 on a shared variable without synchronization. Why might the final count be wrong?
quiz.answer: The read-modify-write steps interleave, losing one update
quiz.explain: count = count + 1 is a read, an add and a write. Both threads can read the same old value before either writes, so one increment disappears. The variable really is shared, and reordering already-atomic writes could not lose a count.
choices: The read-modify-write steps interleave, losing one update
The operating system runs each thread fully before the other
Each thread gets a private copy that leaves the original alone
The increment is atomic, but the two results arrive out of order

quiz.prompt: Virtual memory lets a program use more address space than the physical RAM installed. How is this primarily achieved?
quiz.answer: Pages of memory move between RAM and disk as needed
quiz.explain: The address space is divided into pages, and only the pages in use need a physical frame; the rest sit on disk until they are touched. Swapping whole programs in and out was the older scheme, and nothing about virtual memory compresses an address.
choices: Pages of memory move between RAM and disk as needed
Each program is given the whole of RAM in its turn
Programs are forbidden from using more than the RAM size
Addresses are compressed so more of them fit in memory

quiz.prompt: What is the main reason an operating system runs user programs in a separate 'user mode' rather than giving them full 'kernel mode' access?
quiz.answer: To stop a faulty program touching hardware or other memory
quiz.explain: Privilege separation is about what a program is allowed to touch. Cutting off a runaway loop is the timer interrupt's job, there is one kernel shared by all, and running a foreign instruction set is emulation rather than protection.
choices: To stop a faulty program touching hardware or other memory
So the kernel can interrupt a program that loops forever
So each program gets its own private copy of the kernel
So programs compiled for other CPUs can run alongside

quiz.prompt: Four jobs arrive together at time 0 with CPU bursts of 4, 1, 3 and 2 milliseconds, and a shortest-job-first scheduler runs them without preemption. Give the average waiting time in milliseconds.
quiz.explain: SJF runs 1, 2, 3, 4; the waits are 0, 1, 3 and 6 ms, averaging 10/4 = 2.5 ms, the ordering that minimises average wait.

quiz.prompt: Thread A locks mutex M1 and then waits for M2; thread B locks M2 and then waits for M1. The program freezes. Which single change removes the deadlock?
quiz.answer: Make both threads take the mutexes in the same global order
choices: Make both threads take the mutexes in the same global order
Give each thread its own copy of the two mutexes
Raise the priority of thread A above thread B
Replace the mutexes with one spinlock per thread
quiz.explain: A consistent lock order breaks the circular-wait condition, one of the four conditions a deadlock needs in order to form.

quiz.prompt: A server that handled 100 requests a second slows to 3 a second after a new service starts. Disk activity stays pinned at 100% and the CPU sits mostly idle. What has most likely happened?
quiz.answer: The working set exceeds RAM, so the machine thrashes on page faults
choices: The working set exceeds RAM, so the machine thrashes on page faults
The CPU has overheated and dropped to a much lower clock speed
The new service holds a lock that the old one waits on per request
The network card has started dropping the incoming packets
quiz.explain: Idle CPU plus a saturated disk plus a memory-hungry newcomer is the signature of thrashing: pages get evicted and faulted straight back in. Lock contention and a throttled CPU would both show CPU time being spent, and dropped packets would not touch the disk at all.

quiz.prompt: Four jobs arrive together at time 0 and run first-come first-served without preemption, with CPU bursts of 4, 1, 3 and 2 milliseconds in that order. Give the average waiting time in milliseconds.
quiz.explain: Waits are 0, 4, 5 and 8 milliseconds, summing to 17, and 17 divided by 4 is 4.25 — worse than the 2.5 ms shortest-job-first achieves on the same jobs.

quiz.prompt: A web server that forks a separate process per request runs out of memory under load. Moving to threads inside one process helps mainly because:
quiz.answer: Threads share a single address space, so each costs far less memory
choices: Threads share a single address space, so each costs far less memory
Threads can occupy more cores than processes are allowed to
Threads need no locking at all, so synchronisation overhead disappears
Threads are scheduled by the program rather than by the kernel
quiz.explain: Each process needs its own page tables and its own copy of the address space; threads share one, which is why they are cheap and also why they need locks. Both are scheduled by the kernel and neither is restricted in how many cores it may use.

quiz.prompt: A program sweeps a 1 GB array end to end, over and over, on a machine with 512 MB of RAM under an LRU page policy, and almost every access faults. Which change helps most?
quiz.answer: Process the array in blocks small enough to fit in RAM
choices: Process the array in blocks small enough to fit in RAM
Switch the replacement policy from LRU to first-in first-out
Increase the page size so there are fewer pages to track
Raise the process's scheduling priority
quiz.explain: A repeated linear sweep is the worst case for LRU: every page is evicted just before it is needed again. Blocking restores locality.

quiz.prompt: A logging service loses the last minute of records after a power cut, even though every write() call returned success. Why?
quiz.answer: The bytes sat in the kernel's page cache, not yet on disk
choices: The bytes sat in the kernel's page cache, not yet on disk
write() buffers in the C library until the buffer fills
Journalling rolled the file back to its last checkpoint
The file's length was updated but its contents were not
quiz.explain: A successful write() means the kernel accepted the data, not that a platter or flash cell holds it; durability requires fsync or an equivalent flush. write() is a system call and does no library buffering, and journalling protects file-system structure rather than discarding accepted data.

lesson_media.alt: Two application processes submit work to an operating-system scheduler, which time-slices one CPU, maps each virtual address space to physical memory, and mediates file and device access.
lesson_media.caption: An operating system multiplexes and protects resources. Processes see virtual abstractions; the kernel schedules CPU time, maps memory, and checks requests before drivers access hardware.

nodes.title: Computer Networks
nodes.goal: Protocols, packets and the layered internet.

lesson_media.alt: Four differently colored paths cross two brass router boxes and end at four receiver slots marked with distinct shapes.
lesson_media.caption: IP packets can take different routes and arrive out of order. TCP identifies positions in a byte stream, acknowledges progress and retransmits missing data before delivering an ordered stream to the application.

lesson_media.title: Trace a lost TCP segment
lesson_media.instructions: Advance through a fixed four-segment transfer in which segment 2 is lost. Watch cumulative acknowledgements, receiver buffering, timeout retransmission and ordered release.

quiz.prompt: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery, while UDP does not. For a live video call where occasional lost frames are acceptable but low latency is critical, which is usually preferred?
quiz.answer: UDP-based real-time transport, so the application can manage timing and loss without TCP head-of-line waiting
quiz.explain: For an interactive call, waiting for TCP to retransmit older bytes can make later media arrive too late. A UDP-based real-time protocol can choose concealment, selective repair or frame recovery according to deadlines. Loss can affect dependent predictive frames until a recovery point, so it is not guaranteed to damage only one picture; the tradeoff is controlled latency rather than harmless loss.
choices: UDP-based real-time transport, so the application can manage timing and loss without TCP head-of-line waiting
TCP, since one dropped packet would corrupt the stream
TCP, since its congestion control keeps the picture smooth
UDP, since its shorter header is what saves the time

quiz.prompt: In the layered internet model, what is the main benefit of separating concerns into layers (e.g., IP for addressing, TCP for reliability)?
quiz.answer: Each layer can change on its own if interfaces stay fixed
quiz.explain: Layering is about substitution: IP can run over Ethernet or Wi-Fi through a stable link-layer interface, while TCP in turn uses IP's packet service. The separation costs header bytes rather than saving them, and IP itself does not promise reliable delivery; TCP adds that service above it.
choices: Each layer can change on its own if interfaces stay fixed
It guarantees that no packet gets lost or delayed
Fewer header bytes are needed than in a flat design
Each layer re-checks the data, so no error can survive

quiz.prompt: A file is sent across the internet in many packets that may take different routes. What ensures the receiver reconstructs the data correctly and in order when using TCP?
quiz.answer: TCP byte sequence numbers, cumulative acknowledgements and retransmission
quiz.explain: TCP sequence numbers locate bytes in the stream, and a cumulative ACK normally states the next byte expected. The receiver can buffer later bytes while the sender infers a gap from duplicate ACKs or a timeout and retransmits missing data. IP makes no ordering promise; TCP releases an ordered byte stream to the application.
choices: TCP byte sequence numbers, cumulative acknowledgements and retransmission
IP delivers the packets in the order they were sent
The receiving application sorts the data as it arrives
Routers hold each packet until the earlier ones have passed

quiz.prompt: A /26 IPv4 subnet leaves 6 bits for host addresses. After reserving the network address and the broadcast address, how many usable host addresses remain?
quiz.explain: 6 host bits give 64 addresses; the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address are reserved, leaving 62 for machines.

quiz.prompt: A link carries 100 Mbit/s with a 100 ms round trip. A sender using TCP with a fixed 64 KB window measures only about 5 Mbit/s. Which explanation fits?
quiz.answer: Throughput is capped at the window divided by the round trip
choices: Throughput is capped at the window divided by the round trip
The window is fine; the link is shared twenty ways
Loss forces a retransmission on almost every round trip
The receiver's disk cannot absorb data faster than 5 Mbit/s
quiz.explain: A sender may have only one window of unacknowledged bytes outstanding, so it sends 65,536 bytes then waits a round trip: about 5.2 Mbit/s, exactly what was measured. Window scaling is what lets TCP fill a long fat pipe.

quiz.prompt: An hour ago a site's DNS record changed to a new IP address. Some users reach the new server while others still land on the old one. Which mechanism explains the split?
quiz.answer: Resolvers cache the old record until its TTL expires
choices: Resolvers cache the old record until its TTL expires
TCP retransmits to the address it first connected to
Routers keep the old path in their forwarding tables
Browsers pin a site to whichever server answered first
quiz.explain: DNS answers are cached for the length of their TTL, so a change spreads gradually; lowering the TTL beforehand shortens the split.

quiz.prompt: A 1 Gbit/s link transmits a packet of 12,000 bits. Give the transmission time in microseconds.
quiz.explain: 12,000 bits divided by 10^9 bits per second is 12 microseconds.

quiz.prompt: Two laptops behind one home router both open connections to the same web server, which sees a single public address. How does the router keep the two conversations apart?
quiz.answer: NAPT/PAT maps each private address-and-port flow to a public source port
choices: NAPT/PAT maps each private address-and-port flow to a public source port
It hands each laptop the public address in turn
It queues one laptop's traffic until the other has finished
The server tags each reply with the laptop's MAC address
quiz.explain: Network address and port translation, also called NAPT or PAT, records each private address-and-port flow and assigns it a public-side source port. The returning destination port lets the router restore the correct private endpoint.

quiz.prompt: A workstation reaches every host on its own subnet but nothing outside it. Its configured DNS resolver is also outside that subnet, and DNS lookups fail. Which setting is the first suspect?
quiz.answer: The default gateway
choices: The default gateway
The interface MTU
The MAC address of the network card
The cable between the machine and the switch
quiz.explain: Same-subnet traffic is delivered directly, but every off-subnet destination—including the configured DNS resolver in this scenario—must be reached through the default gateway. A missing or wrong gateway therefore gives exactly this pattern.

quiz.prompt: A download on an idle, fast link starts slowly and reaches full speed only after a few seconds. Which mechanism explains the ramp?
quiz.answer: TCP slow start, which grows the congestion window gradually
choices: TCP slow start, which grows the congestion window gradually
DNS resolution being retried until it succeeds
The server compressing later parts of the file more heavily
The receiver emptying its buffer only after the first second
quiz.explain: A sender has no idea what the path can carry, so it probes upward from a small window rather than flooding the link.

nodes.title: Database Systems
nodes.goal: Transactions, indexing and distributed data.

quiz.prompt: A bank transfer debits one account and credits another. The 'A' in ACID (atomicity) guarantees that:
quiz.answer: Either both the debit and credit happen, or neither
quiz.explain: Atomicity makes a transaction all-or-nothing, so a half-completed transfer can never be committed.
choices: Either both the debit and credit happen, or neither
Multiple transfers can run at exactly the same moment
The data is safely copied to several other servers
The transaction completes within one second

quiz.prompt: A query filtering on a customer's email is slow because the database scans every row. Adding an index on the email column helps because:
quiz.answer: The index finds matching rows without a full scan
quiz.explain: An index is a separate ordered structure over the columns it names; a lookup walks it to the few matching row locations instead of reading every row. It is not a cache of recent reads, it orders only its own columns, and the rows still have to be fetched unless the index already holds every column the query wants.
choices: The index finds matching rows without a full scan
The index keeps the table sorted by every column at once
The index caches whichever rows were read most recently
The index lets the query be answered without touching disk

quiz.prompt: In a distributed database, why can adding an index speed up reads but slow down writes?
quiz.answer: Each write must also update the index, adding work
quiz.explain: Every insert, delete and indexed update has to place the row in the index too, so a write pays once per index the table carries. The structure is edited in place rather than rebuilt, and concurrent readers are not shut out of it.
choices: Each write must also update the index, adding work
The index is rebuilt whenever an indexed row changes
Writes lock the whole index while they are running
Readers and writers cannot use the index at the same time

quiz.prompt: A B-tree index holds 1,000,000 keys and each node has a fan-out of 100, so every extra level multiplies the reachable keys by 100. How many levels must a lookup descend to reach a leaf?
quiz.explain: Fan-out 100 reaches 100, then 10,000, then 1,000,000 keys, so a lookup touches about 3 nodes - the reason B-trees keep disk reads tiny.

quiz.prompt: A report runs SELECT SUM(balance) twice inside one transaction at READ COMMITTED. Between the two reads, another transaction commits a deposit into one of those accounts. What does the report see, and why?
quiz.answer: A larger second total: each statement sees a new snapshot
choices: A larger second total: each statement sees a new snapshot
The same total, because a transaction is atomic
The same total, since READ COMMITTED locks the rows it read
An error, because the rows changed under an open transaction
quiz.explain: READ COMMITTED gives each statement a fresh view of committed data, so the second SUM includes the deposit - a non-repeatable read. Holding one view for the whole transaction is what REPEATABLE READ adds; atomicity governs the transaction's own writes, not what it is shown.

quiz.prompt: A key-value store shards by hash of the key. One key, the homepage counter, takes 40% of all writes, and its shard saturates while the others idle. Which change relieves it?
quiz.answer: Split the counter into sub-keys and sum them on read
choices: Split the counter into sub-keys and sum them on read
Rehash with a different function to move the key elsewhere
Add more shards so the hash spreads the load wider
Replicate the hot shard so reads and writes both spread
quiz.explain: A single key lands on one shard whatever the hash or the shard count, so the fix has to happen in the data model: sharded counters aggregate at read time.

quiz.prompt: A table carries an index on (last_name, first_name). A query that filters only on first_name remains slow. Why?
quiz.answer: The index is sorted on last_name before first_name
choices: The index is sorted on last_name before first_name
The index is used only when both columns are named
A two-column index requires an equality test on first_name
The optimiser ignores the last_name index once the table grows
quiz.explain: Entries are ordered by last_name and only then by first_name, so rows sharing a first_name are scattered all through the index with no contiguous range to scan. A query on last_name alone uses it perfectly well, which is why the leading column is the one that matters.

quiz.prompt: A table holds 10,000,000 rows and a query returns 8,000,000 of them, so the planner prefers a full scan to the index. What percentage of the rows does the query return?
quiz.explain: 8,000,000 out of 10,000,000 is 80%, far above the few percent at which an index still pays.

quiz.prompt: Two transactions each update rows A and B but in opposite order, and one is aborted with a deadlock error. Which change stops it recurring?
quiz.answer: Have both transactions lock the rows in one agreed order
choices: Have both transactions lock the rows in one agreed order
Raise the lock timeout so each can wait longer
Run both at a lower isolation level
Add an index on the columns being updated
quiz.explain: A deadlock needs a cycle in the wait-for graph; a global lock ordering makes such a cycle impossible.

quiz.prompt: A user updates their profile, is redirected, and immediately sees their old details. Writes go to a primary and reads are spread over replicas that lag by about two seconds. Explain the cause and one fix.
quiz.answer: The write reached the primary but the following read was routed to a replica that had not yet applied it, so the user saw stale data; route reads that follow a user's own write to the primary, or make the client wait until the replica has caught up to the write's position.
quiz.explain: This is a read-your-writes consistency failure, a normal consequence of asynchronous replication rather than a bug in the write.

lesson_media.alt: Three panels connect a balanced index path to fewer page reads, a debit-credit transaction to atomic commit, and replicated log positions to a stated consistency rule.
lesson_media.caption: Database mechanisms solve different problems: indexes accelerate access, transactions preserve declared invariants, and replication improves availability or scale under an explicit consistency protocol.

nodes.title: Machine Learning
nodes.goal: Learning from data: regression, classification, neural nets.

quiz.prompt: A model scores 99% on its training data and 70% on held-out data - a textbook case of overfitting. The team adds a strong regularisation penalty and retrains. If the diagnosis is right, what should the two numbers do?
quiz.answer: Training falls, held-out rises
quiz.explain: Regularisation trades fit on the training set for generalisation, so the gap closes from both sides. If training accuracy stayed at 99% nothing about the memorisation would have changed, and if both moved the same way the gap would point to something other than overfitting.
choices: Training falls, held-out rises
Both rise, since the model is now better tuned
Training stays at 99% while held-out rises
Held-out falls too, since the model has less capacity

quiz.prompt: A team turns 'predict a house's price' into a classification task by bucketing prices into ten ranges and predicting the bucket. What do they give up compared with treating it as regression?
quiz.answer: A near miss and a wild miss now count the same
quiz.explain: A plain classifier treats its ten classes as unrelated names, so predicting bucket 1 when the truth is bucket 10 costs exactly what predicting bucket 9 costs; both the ordering and the size of the error are thrown away. Bucketing changes the target only, not what the inputs may be.
choices: A near miss and a wild miss now count the same
The model can no longer use numeric features as inputs
Nothing important: ten buckets describe a price well enough
The buckets are ordered, so the classifier will respect that order

quiz.prompt: A team has 50,000 product photos and no labels at all. Which of these can they still attempt without labelling anything first?
quiz.answer: Grouping the images into visually similar clusters
quiz.explain: Clustering finds structure in the inputs alone, which is what makes it unsupervised. Everything else needs a target: a category to fit, a correct answer to score against, or a price to explain.
choices: Grouping the images into visually similar clusters
Measuring how accurately a classifier names each product
Training a model to predict each photo's product category
Ranking which features most affect the predicted price

quiz.prompt: A spam filter is tested on 1,000 emails. It flags 120 as spam, of which 90 really are spam, and 60 genuine spam emails slip through unflagged. Give the filter's precision as a decimal.
quiz.explain: Precision counts how many flagged items were right: 90/120 = 0.75. Recall differs here - 90 of the 150 real spam messages, or 0.6.

quiz.prompt: A team scales every feature using the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset, then splits it into train and test. Test accuracy looks excellent; production accuracy does not. Which flaw explains the gap?
quiz.answer: Test statistics leaked into training through the shared scaling
choices: Test statistics leaked into training through the shared scaling
Scaling strips information the model needed to generalise
The split should have happened before the data was gathered
Standard deviation is the wrong statistic for scaling features
quiz.explain: Preprocessing has to be fitted on the training split alone and then applied to the test split; otherwise the test set has already shaped the model and the estimate flatters it.

quiz.prompt: A model predicting a disease that affects 1 person in 1,000 reports 99.9% accuracy. Which check would reveal whether it learned anything?
quiz.answer: Compare it against a model that predicts 'healthy' for everyone
choices: Compare it against a model that predicts 'healthy' for everyone
Retrain it on twice as much data and compare the accuracy
Measure accuracy again on a second random sample
Check that the training and test sets match in size
quiz.explain: The always-negative baseline also scores 99.9%, so accuracy carries no information here; recall and precision on the positive class do.

quiz.prompt: A test set holds 200 positive cases. A model flags 150 items in total, of which 120 are genuinely positive. Give the recall as a decimal.
quiz.explain: Recall is true positives over all actual positives: 120 divided by 200 is 0.6.

quiz.prompt: A fraud model at a 0.5 threshold catches very few frauds. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 raises recall. What is the expected cost?
quiz.answer: More false alarms, so precision falls
choices: More false alarms, so precision falls
Recall on the training set drops as well
The model has to be retrained from scratch
Accuracy rises, since more cases are caught
quiz.explain: A lower threshold flags more items, which catches more real fraud but also sweeps in more legitimate transactions.

quiz.prompt: Only 200 labelled examples exist, and a single 80/20 split gives a wildly different accuracy each time it is reshuffled. Which practice gives a more trustworthy estimate?
quiz.answer: k-fold cross-validation, averaging the score across folds
choices: k-fold cross-validation, averaging the score across folds
Training on all 200 and reporting accuracy on the same data
Using a 99/1 split so training sees almost everything
Keeping the split that produced the best score
quiz.explain: With a tiny test set, one split is mostly noise. Cross-validation uses every example for testing exactly once and averages away that noise.

quiz.prompt: A linear model shows high error on both its training set and its validation set. Which step is most likely to help?
quiz.answer: Add features or move to a more expressive model
choices: Add features or move to a more expressive model
Collect more training rows of the same kind
Increase the regularisation strength so the model generalises better
Stop training earlier than before
quiz.explain: High training error means underfitting; the three rejected options all fight overfitting and would make underfitting worse.

lesson_media.alt: A supervised-learning pipeline separates labelled examples into training and held-out sets, adjusts parameters to reduce training loss, then measures unseen prediction errors without training on them.
lesson_media.caption: Machine learning estimates a rule from data rather than receiving every case explicitly. Held-out evaluation tests generalization; leakage or a shifted population can make a high score misleading.

nodes.title: Security & Cryptography
nodes.goal: Encryption, hashing and threat models.

quiz.prompt: In public-key cryptography, Alice wants to send Bob a message only he can read. Which key does she use to encrypt it?
quiz.answer: Bob's public key
quiz.explain: Encrypting with Bob's public key means only Bob's matching private key can decrypt it, ensuring confidentiality.
choices: Alice's public key
Alice's private key
Bob's private key
Bob's public key

quiz.prompt: A site stores each password as hash(salt + password) with a fresh random salt per user, and keeps the salts in the clear beside the hashes. Why does storing the salts openly not defeat the point?
quiz.answer: The salt stops one table cracking every account at once
quiz.explain: A salt is not a secret; its job is to make every user's stored hash unique, so a precomputed rainbow table and a single guess-and-compare pass no longer cover many accounts at once. The attacker has to attack each account separately, and that is what buys time.
choices: The salt stops one table cracking every account at once
The salt is useless to an attacker who cannot read the hashes
The salt is hashed too, so it is not really in the clear
The salt is long enough that guessing it stays infeasible

quiz.prompt: A message arrives carrying a digital signature that verifies against Bob's public key. Which of these has the valid signature established?
quiz.answer: It is unchanged and came from that key
quiz.explain: A signature binds the content to the private key, so tampering and forgery are detectable. It does not encrypt the message, it does not stop the same signed message being captured and resent later, and it says nothing about which human was at the keyboard.
choices: It is unchanged and came from that key
It was unreadable to anyone who intercepted it
It was sent recently rather than replayed later
Bob read the message himself before it was sent

quiz.prompt: A password is 4 characters long and each character comes from a 62-character alphabet. Give the exact number of candidates an exhaustive search must try in the worst case.
quiz.explain: 62^4 = 14,776,336, which a modern GPU works through in well under a second - the reason length matters more than character variety.

quiz.prompt: A login form builds its SQL by pasting strings together. An attacker types  ' OR '1'='1  as the password and gets in. Which fix actually closes the hole?
quiz.answer: Use parameterised queries, so input never becomes SQL syntax
choices: Strip single quotes from the input before building the query
Use parameterised queries, so input never becomes SQL syntax
Hash the password before placing it into the query string
Limit the password box to 20 characters in the browser
quiz.explain: Parameter binding keeps data out of the parsed statement. Character filtering is bypassable, browser limits are client-side, and hashing leaves other fields injectable.

quiz.prompt: Two systems compare a submitted API token with the stored one. System A uses ==, which stops at the first differing byte; system B compares every byte regardless. What advantage does B have?
quiz.answer: Its constant running time leaks nothing about the stored token
choices: Its constant running time leaks nothing about the stored token
It rejects forged tokens that happen to share a prefix
It uses less CPU, because the comparison has no branches
It stops an attacker from submitting many guesses
quiz.explain: An early-exit comparison takes longer the more leading bytes match, letting an attacker recover the token byte by byte; constant-time comparison removes that side channel.

quiz.prompt: A browser warns that a site's certificate is signed by an authority it does not know, and the user clicks through. What risk has been accepted?
quiz.answer: Someone in the middle may be decrypting and re-encrypting it all
choices: Someone in the middle may be decrypting and re-encrypting it all
The connection carries no encryption at all until a known authority signs it
The certificate has expired, so the site's own keys are stale
Anyone who captured the traffic could decrypt it afterwards
quiz.explain: Encryption without an authenticated identity protects the channel to whoever is at the other end - and that may be the attacker whose certificate was presented. The traffic is still encrypted, but it is encrypted to them; an unknown signer is a different complaint from an expired one.

quiz.prompt: A hash function produces 256-bit outputs. By the birthday bound a collision is expected after about 2^k random trials. Give k.
quiz.explain: The birthday bound is about the square root of the output space, which is 2^(256/2) = 2^128.

quiz.prompt: A user's password appears in a public breach dump, yet the attacker still cannot sign in. Which control most likely stopped them?
quiz.answer: A second factor generated on the user's phone
choices: A second factor generated on the user's phone
The site storing passwords salted and hashed rather than in plain text
The site rate-limiting failed login attempts
The password being long and hard to guess
quiz.explain: Salting, rate limits and length all resist guessing; none of them helps once the correct password is already known.

quiz.prompt: A messaging app uses public-key cryptography only to agree a short random key, then encrypts the whole conversation with that key. Why not use public-key cryptography throughout?
quiz.answer: Public-key operations are orders of magnitude slower on bulk data
choices: Public-key operations are orders of magnitude slower on bulk data
A public-key cipher can encrypt only one message per key
The public key would then have to be kept secret
Symmetric keys are harder for an attacker to intercept while in transit
quiz.explain: Hybrid encryption takes the key-distribution benefit of public-key cryptography and the speed of a symmetric cipher. The symmetric key is the harder thing to move safely, which is precisely why the public-key step exists.

lesson_media.alt: Encryption maps plaintext and a secret key plus nonce to ciphertext that the key can reverse, while hashing maps a message to a fixed digest and a threat model states the attacker capabilities.
lesson_media.caption: Encryption provides confidentiality only under assumptions about keys, nonces, algorithms, and attackers. Cryptographic hashes are designed for one-way integrity uses, not reversible secrecy.

nodes.title: Systems Programming
nodes.goal: Memory, pointers and building close to the metal.

quiz.prompt: In C, a pointer holds a memory address. If p points to an integer and you write *p = 5, what happens?
quiz.answer: The integer at the address p points to is set to 5
quiz.explain: The * dereferences: it names the object at the address, so the write lands in that object and p itself is untouched. Changing p would be p = 5 and moving it along would be p = p + 5.
choices: The integer at the address p points to is set to 5
The pointer p is changed to hold the address 5
p is moved along to the fifth integer after it
A copy of what p points to is made and set to 5

quiz.prompt: A program calls malloc to allocate memory but never calls free when done, repeatedly. What is the consequence?
quiz.answer: A memory leak: the program's memory use grows over time
quiz.explain: Nothing reclaims a heap block until free is called, so a long-running program's footprint climbs until allocation fails. The exit-time cleanup is real, which is exactly why a leak in a short script is harmless and the same leak in a server is not.
choices: A memory leak: the program's memory use grows over time
The operating system reclaims each block when the loop ends
The program crashes as soon as the first block is lost
Nothing, since the memory is all freed when the program exits

quiz.prompt: A C program compiles with no errors or warnings, then crashes on one particular input. What does the clean compile actually tell you about the program?
quiz.answer: Only that it obeys the language's rules
quiz.explain: A compiler checks syntax and the static rules of the type system and then emits machine code; whether that code does the right thing on a given input is outside what it inspects. C adds no run-time type checking at all, and unreachable code compiles as happily as anything else.
choices: Only that it obeys the language's rules
That the crash must come from the operating system
That its types are checked again while it runs
That every line in it will run at least once

quiz.prompt: In C an int occupies 4 bytes. A pointer p holds the address 1000 and points to an int. What address does p + 3 refer to?
quiz.explain: Pointer arithmetic scales by the pointed-to type, so p + 3 moves 3 x 4 = 12 bytes along, to 1012 rather than 1003.

quiz.prompt: A C function declares a local array, returns its address, and the caller reads through that pointer, seeing garbage. Which explanation fits?
quiz.answer: The array lived in the stack frame that was reclaimed on return
choices: The array lived in the stack frame that was reclaimed on return
The compiler copied the array, so the caller sees a stale copy
Arrays decay to pointers, so the address came back as zero
The array needed malloc, since locals live in read-only memory
quiz.explain: A local lives in the callee's stack frame, which is reclaimed the moment the function returns, so the pointer dangles. Allocating on the heap or letting the caller supply the buffer fixes it.

quiz.prompt: Two loops add up the same 10,000 by 10,000 array of ints. Loop R walks row by row, loop C walks column by column. In C, which stores arrays row-major, loop C runs several times slower. Why?
quiz.answer: Each column step jumps a whole row, so most cache lines get used once
choices: Each column step jumps a whole row, so most cache lines get used once
The compiler cannot unroll a loop whose fastest index is the outer one
Column access needs a multiplication that row access avoids
The CPU must transpose each column into a row before adding
quiz.explain: Row-major layout puts a row's elements next to each other, so striding down a column touches a fresh cache line every step and wastes the rest of each line fetched. Both loops do the same arithmetic and the same number of additions.

quiz.prompt: In C on a typical machine a char takes 1 byte and an int takes 4 bytes and must sit at a 4-byte boundary. A struct holds a char, then an int, then a char, and is padded to a multiple of 4 bytes. How many bytes does it occupy?
quiz.explain: 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding, then 4 for the int, then 1 for the char and 3 more of tail padding: 12 in all.

quiz.prompt: A C function declares a 10 MB array as a local variable and the program crashes the moment the function is entered. Which fix is right?
quiz.answer: Allocate the buffer on the heap with malloc
choices: Allocate the buffer on the heap with malloc
Split it into ten local arrays of one megabyte each
Mark it const so it moves to read-only memory
Zero the array before use so its pages exist
quiz.explain: Stack size is typically a megabyte or so per thread; large buffers belong on the heap, where the limit is far higher.

quiz.prompt: A C program reads input with gets() into a 64-byte array, an attacker supplies 200 bytes, and the attacker gains control of execution. Which property of C makes this possible?
quiz.answer: Array writes are not bounds-checked at run time
choices: Array writes are not bounds-checked at run time
The array was declared without an initial value
Local arrays are placed in read-only memory
The compiler removed the length check as an optimisation
quiz.explain: C trusts the programmer, so writing past the end of a stack array quietly overwrites whatever follows, including the return address.

quiz.prompt: Two C source files each define a global variable with the same name, and the linker rejects the build with a duplicate symbol error. Which change resolves it while keeping both files compiling?
quiz.answer: Mark each definition static so it stays local to its file
choices: Mark each definition static so it stays local to its file
Rename the variable in one file's header only
Declare the variable extern in both files
Compile the two files separately and never link them
quiz.explain: static at file scope gives a global internal linkage, so each translation unit keeps its own copy and the names no longer clash.

lesson_media.alt: A C-like trace stores integer x at address 0x1000, points p at that address, writes 43 through p, and shows x changing from 42 to 43 in the same memory cell.
lesson_media.caption: A pointer value is an address interpreted with a type. Dereferencing accesses the pointed-to object only while its lifetime and bounds are valid; an invalid address causes undefined behavior in C.

nodes.title: Computational Complexity
nodes.goal: P, NP, and the hardest questions in the field.

lesson_media.alt: One input feeds three separate tracks whose work grows linearly, quadratically and exponentially; beside them, a small Boolean assignment is checked against a fixed formula.
lesson_media.caption: Growth rates compare how resource use scales with input size. Separately, a satisfying assignment is a certificate that can be checked quickly; neither picture settles the open P versus NP question.

lesson_media.title: Compare growth and verify a certificate
lesson_media.instructions: Change n to compare n, n squared and 2 to the n from 4 through 20. Then test assignments for the fixed SAT example and distinguish finding a certificate from checking one.

quiz.prompt: A problem is NP-complete. Which statement best captures what that means?
quiz.answer: It is in NP, and every NP problem polynomial-time reduces to it
quiz.explain: NP-complete problems are both in NP and NP-hard: every problem in NP has a polynomial-time reduction to one. A polynomial-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem would therefore give polynomial-time algorithms for all problems in NP.
choices: It is in NP, and every NP problem polynomial-time reduces to it
It resists solution by any known algorithm
It can be solved quickly yet checked rather slowly
It provably requires exponential time to solve

quiz.prompt: SAT is in NP: a proposed satisfying assignment is a certificate that a deterministic verifier can check in polynomial time. A colleague argues that this alone proves SAT can be solved in polynomial time. Where does the argument break?
quiz.answer: Fast verification alone does not provide a polynomial-time way to find a certificate
choices: Fast verification alone does not provide a polynomial-time way to find a certificate
Checking one assignment is not actually polynomial
A fast check would place SAT in P rather than in NP
An unsatisfiable formula has no certificate to check
quiz.explain: NP bounds the cost of verifying a supplied witness; that definition does not itself provide an efficient search algorithm. Whether every efficiently verifiable certificate can also be found in polynomial time is the open P versus NP question. Brute-force search over assignments is one method, but no theorem says every SAT algorithm must use it.

quiz.prompt: Suppose someone finds a polynomial-time algorithm for one NP-complete problem. What would follow?
quiz.answer: P would equal NP, so every NP problem would be solvable in polynomial time
quiz.explain: Every NP problem polynomial-time reduces to an NP-complete problem. Combining those reductions with the new polynomial-time algorithm would put all of NP in P; since P is already a subset of NP, this would prove P = NP.
choices: Just that one problem becomes easy; the rest stay hard
It would prove that the halting problem is decidable
It would immediately prove that P is not equal to NP
P would equal NP, so every NP problem would be solvable in polynomial time

quiz.prompt: An algorithm's running time satisfies T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + n. The master theorem gives a bound of the form n^p * (log n)^q with whole-number exponents p and q. Give p + q.
quiz.explain: The master theorem solves recurrences of the form T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) against n^(log_b a): if f(n) grows slower, T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)); if it grows faster, T(n) = Theta(f(n)); if the two match (case 2), T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) * log n). Here the recurrence coefficients are a=2 and b=2, so n^(log_2 2) = n, matching f(n) = n. Thus T(n) = Theta(n log n), whose requested exponents are p=1 and q=1.

quiz.prompt: You want to show that problem B is NP-hard, and you have a polynomial-time reduction to hand. In which direction must the reduction run?
quiz.answer: From a known NP-hard problem to B
choices: From a known NP-hard problem to B
From B to a known NP-hard problem
From B to a problem already known to lie in P
In either direction, since reductions compose both ways
quiz.explain: Reducing a hard problem A to B shows B is at least as hard as A. Reducing B to something hard shows only that B is no harder, which proves nothing.

quiz.prompt: For a graph on 40 vertices, you must decide exactly whether it has a vertex cover of size at most k=5. Which approach gives an exact fixed-parameter algorithm?
quiz.answer: Branch on an uncovered edge; O(2^k poly(n)) is exact for k=5
choices: Branch on an uncovered edge; O(2^k poly(n)) is exact for k=5
A greedy pass that repeatedly removes the highest-degree vertex, then stops
A 2-approximation of the cover from a maximal matching
An integer program handed to its linear relaxation alone
quiz.explain: Every vertex cover must contain at least one endpoint of any uncovered edge. Branching on those two choices decreases k by one, giving an O(2^k poly(n)) decision algorithm. It is exact for the stated k=5 instance; its usefulness depends on k being small, not on a claim that small k is usual. A 2-approximation has a ratio guarantee but does not decide this exact bound.

quiz.prompt: A logistics team says only that its 5,000-task scheduling problem is NP-hard and asks for a guaranteed optimum by Friday. Which response is technically sound?
quiz.answer: Identify the exact variant, then use a proven approximation if one exists or an exact solver with a time limit and optimality gap
choices: Identify the exact variant, then use a proven approximation if one exists or an exact solver with a time limit and optimality gap
Note that 5,000 tasks is small, so the exponential term stays manageable
Explain that NP-hard problems admit no correct algorithm at any size
Buy faster hardware, since NP-hardness concerns only constant factors
quiz.explain: Approximation guarantees are problem-specific, so 'NP-hard scheduling' is not enough to promise one. An exact mixed-integer or constraint solver can report an incumbent and a bound, making any remaining optimality gap explicit at the deadline. NP-hardness does not prove that every instance is slow, and the absence of a polynomial-time exact algorithm is conditional on P not equaling NP, which remains unproved.

quiz.prompt: An algorithm satisfies T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n, so the master theorem gives T(n) = Theta(n^c). Give c to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The master theorem solves T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) against n^(log_b a): here a=3, b=2, so n^(log_2 3), and since f(n) = n grows slower than n^(log_2 3) (case 1), the recursive splitting dominates and T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)). c is log base 2 of 3, which is 1.5849..., and the linear combining term is dominated by it.

quiz.prompt: A satisfying assignment is a polynomial-size certificate that verifies SAT instances quickly. What is currently known about an analogous certificate for every unsatisfiable Boolean formula?
quiz.answer: No polynomial-size certificate verifiable in polynomial time is known for every UNSAT instance
choices: No polynomial-size certificate verifiable in polynomial time is known for every UNSAT instance
Every one of the 2^n assignments has been proved necessary to check
SAT's certificate automatically puts UNSAT in NP as well
UNSAT has been proved to lie outside NP
quiz.explain: UNSAT is coNP-complete. We do not know whether every UNSAT instance has a polynomial-size certificate accepted by a polynomial-time verifier; equivalently, we do not know whether UNSAT is in NP. In fact, UNSAT is in NP if and only if NP = coNP. SAT's usual satisfying-assignment certificate does not settle that question, and exhaustive search has not been proved necessary.

quiz.prompt: A student gives a polynomial-time reduction from their problem C to 3-SAT and concludes that C is NP-hard. What has the reduction actually shown?
quiz.answer: Only that C is no harder than 3-SAT
choices: Only that C is no harder than 3-SAT
That C is NP-hard, as claimed
That C is NP-complete
That 3-SAT can be solved by solving C
quiz.explain: Hardness needs the reduction to run from a known hard problem into C; reducing C into 3-SAT bounds C from above instead.

nodes.title: Deep Learning & AI
nodes.goal: Transformers, training and modern AI.

quiz.prompt: The self-attention mechanism in a transformer lets the model, when processing one token, do what?
quiz.answer: Draw information from other tokens based on relevance
quiz.explain: Attention weights come from learned query-key similarity, so relevance rather than distance or a fixed window decides what gets read. Restricting the view to earlier tokens is a masking choice made in decoder models, not a property of attention itself.
choices: Draw information from other tokens based on relevance
Combine the tokens inside a fixed-size window around it
Read the tokens before it, but never those after it
Weight the other tokens by how close they sit in the sequence

quiz.prompt: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards through the network to get the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight. In a deep stack whose layers each multiply the backward signal by a factor well below 1, what happens to the gradients that reach the earliest layers?
quiz.answer: They shrink towards zero
quiz.explain: The chain rule multiplies the per-layer factors together, so many factors below 1 make the product vanish long before it reaches the first layer - the vanishing-gradient problem. Factors above 1 give the opposite, exploding gradients; the rule itself stays exact either way.
choices: They shrink towards zero
They grow at every step
They become undefined once the factors drop below 1
They stay the same size, since the chain rule is exact

quiz.prompt: A key architectural advantage of transformers over earlier recurrent networks (RNNs) for long sequences is:
quiz.answer: They process all positions in parallel, not in sequence
quiz.explain: Attention removes the sequential dependency, so a whole sequence trains in one pass. The price is that a layer's attention cost grows with the square of the length rather than linearly, transformers are famously data-hungry, and they carry no recurrent hidden state at all.
choices: They process all positions in parallel, not in sequence
They need far less training data than a recurrent network
Their cost per layer grows linearly with the sequence length
They keep a hidden state that never has to be reset

quiz.prompt: One self-attention head projects a model width of 512 into query, key and value vectors of width 64 each, using three weight matrices of shape 512 by 64 and no biases. How many parameters do those projections hold?
quiz.explain: Each projection is 512 x 64 = 32,768 parameters and there are three of them, so 98,304 in total.

quiz.prompt: Doubling a transformer's context from 2,048 to 4,096 tokens multiplies the size of one attention layer's score matrix by what factor, and why?
quiz.answer: Four times, since the matrix carries one entry per ordered token pair
choices: Four times, since the matrix carries one entry per ordered token pair
Twice, since each token attends to a fixed-size neighbourhood
Twice, since the parameter count scales with sequence length
Eight times, since attention runs once per layer and per head
quiz.explain: Self-attention forms an n by n score matrix, so cost grows with n squared; the parameter count itself does not depend on sequence length.

quiz.prompt: Training loss falls steadily while validation loss falls, flattens, then climbs from epoch 12 onwards. Which intervention addresses the observed problem most directly?
quiz.answer: Stop at the validation minimum and keep those weights
choices: Stop at the validation minimum and keep those weights
Raise the learning rate so the model escapes the plateau
Add more layers so the model can fit the data better
Train for many more epochs so validation loss recovers
quiz.explain: A rising validation curve alongside a falling training curve is overfitting; early stopping or stronger regularisation is the direct remedy, while extra capacity makes it worse.

quiz.prompt: A fully connected layer maps 1,024 inputs to 256 outputs and has one bias per output. Give the number of parameters.
quiz.explain: 1,024 x 256 = 262,144 weights, plus 256 biases, giving 262,400.

quiz.prompt: Training loss becomes NaN a few hundred steps into a run with a large learning rate. Which intervention addresses the cause most directly?
quiz.answer: Lower the learning rate and clip the gradient norm
choices: Lower the learning rate and clip the gradient norm
Raise the batch size until the loss settles
Add more layers so the network has capacity for the loss
Replace the cross-entropy loss with accuracy
quiz.explain: NaN loss usually follows an exploding update that overflows the weights; smaller steps and clipped gradients bound the update size.

quiz.prompt: A 60-layer plain convolutional network reaches a worse training loss than an otherwise identical 20-layer one. Which diagnosis and fix fit that observation?
quiz.answer: Depth degrades the signal, so residual connections should be added
choices: Depth degrades the signal, so residual connections should be added
The dataset is too small for the deeper model and should be enlarged
The learning rate is too small and should be raised tenfold
The deeper model overfits, so dropout should be added
quiz.explain: Worse training loss, not worse validation loss, rules out overfitting: a deeper network can express everything the shallower one can, so failing to fit is an optimisation problem. This is the degradation problem that residual blocks were introduced to solve.

quiz.prompt: A deployed transformer answers well on short prompts but degrades sharply beyond the length it was trained on, with errors that depend on token position. Which cause fits?
quiz.answer: Positional encodings were never trained at those offsets
choices: Positional encodings were never trained at those offsets
The vocabulary contains no tokens for long inputs
Attention cost grows quadratically, which lowers accuracy
The weights are quantised differently at long sequence lengths
quiz.explain: Extrapolating past the trained context puts the model in a positional regime it never saw; cost growth is a speed problem, not an accuracy one.

lesson_media.alt: A transformer pipeline turns tokens into vectors, uses attention to mix context-dependent information, predicts next-token probabilities, computes loss against a target and propagates gradients to update parameters.
lesson_media.caption: Transformers learn parameters by optimizing prediction loss over examples. Attention forms weighted combinations of representations; a fluent output is still a probabilistic model result, not a guarantee of truth.

nodes.title: Distributed Systems
nodes.goal: Consensus, replication and fault tolerance at scale.

quiz.prompt: A partition splits a five-node cluster into a three-node side and a two-node side. The cluster is configured to require a majority quorum for every write. What happens on each side while the partition lasts?
quiz.answer: The larger side accepts writes; the smaller side refuses
quiz.explain: A majority quorum is the CP choice under CAP: three of five is a majority, so that side stays available and consistent while the minority must refuse rather than diverge. Accepting on both sides is the AP choice, which this configuration has explicitly given up.
choices: The larger side accepts writes; the smaller side refuses
Both sides accept writes and reconcile once the link returns
Both sides refuse writes until the partition has healed
The two-node side accepts writes, having less to reconcile

quiz.prompt: Raft commits an entry only once a majority of the cluster has stored it. Three nodes of a five-node cluster fail. What can the two survivors still do?
quiz.answer: Serve reads, but commit nothing new
quiz.explain: A majority of five is three, so two nodes can neither elect a leader nor commit an entry; what they already hold is still there to read. Consensus trades availability for the guarantee that two majorities can never disagree.
choices: Serve reads, but commit nothing new
Commit new entries once the two of them agree
Elect a leader and carry on as a two-node cluster
Nothing: the committed log is lost with the majority

quiz.prompt: A service keeps three replicas of its data so that it survives one crash. To save money the team moves all three replicas onto one physical host. What has that cost them?
quiz.answer: The host is now a single point of failure
quiz.explain: Redundancy buys fault tolerance only when the copies fail independently. Three replicas on one host share its power supply, its kernel and its disk controller, so a single failure takes all three; the quorum logic and the consistency it provides are untouched.
choices: The host is now a single point of failure
Consistency, because replicas on one host cannot form a quorum
Nothing, as long as the three processes stay independent
Only latency, since replication traffic no longer leaves the host

quiz.prompt: A replicated store keeps 5 copies of each record and uses quorum reads and writes with W = 3. Give the smallest R that guarantees every read overlaps every completed write.
quiz.explain: Quorum overlap needs R + W > N. With N = 5 and W = 3, R must exceed 2, so R = 3.

quiz.prompt: A payment service retries any request that times out, and customers occasionally get charged twice. Which change fixes that without giving up retries?
quiz.answer: Have clients send an idempotency key the server deduplicates on
choices: Have clients send an idempotency key the server deduplicates on
Increase the timeout so requests have longer to complete
Move the transport from HTTP to a durable message queue
Wrap the charge in a database transaction before replying
quiz.explain: A timeout is ambiguous - the first request may already have succeeded. A deduplication key turns the retry into a no-op, the standard way to get exactly-once effects over at-least-once delivery.

quiz.prompt: Two datacentres lose the link between them, and an operator insists both sides keep accepting writes to the same shopping-cart keys. What must the system then accept?
quiz.answer: Divergent replicas that need merging when the link returns
choices: Divergent replicas that need merging when the link returns
A pause in writes until a majority forms on one side
Loss of durability for the writes taken during the split
A rollback of both sides to the last shared snapshot
quiz.explain: Choosing availability during a partition means each side proceeds alone, so replicas diverge and need conflict resolution - CRDTs, last-write-wins or an application merge - once healed.

quiz.prompt: Two replicas hold conflicting values for one key, and their wall-clock timestamps disagree because the machine clocks drift. Which mechanism decides whether one update genuinely happened before the other?
quiz.answer: Version vectors, which record causal history
choices: Version vectors, which record causal history
NTP-synchronised timestamps at millisecond precision
A leader election run once the conflict is noticed
Keeping whichever replica holds the larger value
quiz.explain: Physical clocks cannot establish causality across machines; version vectors track what each replica had seen when it wrote.

quiz.prompt: A Raft cluster has 7 nodes and needs a majority to make progress. How many nodes may fail while the cluster still commits entries?
quiz.explain: A majority of 7 is 4, so the cluster survives 7 - 4 = 3 failures.

quiz.prompt: A team advertises that their message queue delivers each message exactly once from producer to consumer. Which framing of that claim is accurate?
quiz.answer: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives that effect
choices: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives that effect
Exactly-once holds as long as the consumer acknowledges before processing
Exactly-once requires only that the network never drops a message
Exactly-once delivery follows from acknowledgements alone
quiz.explain: A crash between delivery and acknowledgement is indistinguishable from a lost message, so duplicates must be tolerated at the consumer. Acknowledging first turns the ambiguity into lost work instead - at-most-once - and no amount of network reliability removes the crash window.

quiz.prompt: After a brief outage, 10,000 clients all retry at the same instant and knock the recovering service down again. Which change breaks the cycle?
quiz.answer: Exponential backoff with random jitter
choices: Exponential backoff with random jitter
A fixed one-second retry interval for every client
Raising the server's connection limit
Retrying twice as fast so the backlog drains sooner
quiz.explain: Synchronised retries are the problem; jitter spreads them in time and backoff lowers the total rate as failures persist.

lesson_media.alt: A three-node replicated log accepts command x equals 7 at the leader, receives one follower acknowledgement while another follower is offline, reaches a two-of-three majority and then commits entry 42.
