lesson_media.caption: In a majority-based consensus protocol, replication to a quorum can allow progress despite one unavailable node. Exact safety also depends on term, log-matching, and leader-election rules not compressed into this trace.

nodes.title: Programming Language Theory
nodes.goal: Type systems, semantics and the lambda calculus.

quiz.prompt: A static type system rejects the program before it runs when types don't match. What is the primary benefit?
quiz.answer: A whole class of errors is caught before it runs
quiz.explain: Static typing detects type errors before running, preventing an entire category of runtime failures.
choices: A whole class of errors is caught before it runs
It removes the need to write tests for the program
It lets any variable hold values of any type at any time
The program runs faster than a dynamically typed one

quiz.prompt: In the untyped lambda calculus, the term (λx. x x) (λx. x x) gets beta-reduced over and over. What happens?
quiz.answer: It reduces to itself forever and has no normal form
choices: It reduces in one step to the identity function
It gets stuck, since x occurs free in the body
It reduces to itself forever and has no normal form
It reaches a normal form after two beta steps
quiz.explain: This term, Ω, beta-reduces to itself, so reduction never terminates: the untyped calculus is not strongly normalising.

quiz.prompt: Two teams implement the same language from one formal semantics, and their compilers disagree on what a program prints. What does having that semantics let them do?
quiz.answer: Say which compiler is wrong
quiz.explain: A formal semantics fixes the meaning of the language itself, so an implementation can be judged against it rather than being the definition. It settles meaning, not speed; typing is a separate layer; and no semantics decides termination for an arbitrary program.
choices: Say which compiler is wrong
Time both compilers
Prove that the program itself terminates
Reject the program as ill-typed before either runs

quiz.prompt: Under call-by-value an argument is evaluated once before the call; under call-by-name it is re-evaluated at each use. The function f(x) = x + x is applied to g(3), and g prints a line every time it runs. Give the number of lines printed under call-by-name.
quiz.explain: Call-by-name substitutes the unevaluated argument, so g(3) runs once per use of x, twice in all. Call-by-value would run it once, and call-by-need also once because it memoises.

quiz.prompt: A language's type checker accepts a program that then crashes at run time by adding an integer to a function. Which theorem has failed for that language?
quiz.answer: Soundness: well-typed programs do not get stuck
choices: Soundness: well-typed programs do not get stuck
Completeness: the checker accepts every safe program
Decidability: type checking terminates on every input
Principality: each term has a most general type
quiz.explain: Soundness combines progress and preservation, so a well-typed term never reaches a stuck state. A crash in a well-typed program is exactly a soundness failure.

quiz.prompt:
Consider this pseudocode:

  x = 1
  function f(): return x
  function g():
    var x = 2
    return f()

What does g() return under lexical scoping, and what under dynamic scoping?
quiz.answer: 1 under lexical scoping and 2 under dynamic scoping
choices: 1 under lexical scoping and 2 under dynamic scoping
2 under lexical scoping and 1 under dynamic
1 under either rule
2 under either rule
quiz.explain: Lexical scoping resolves x where f was written, finding the global 1; dynamic scoping resolves it in the caller's live environment, finding g's 2.

quiz.prompt: A language lets an Array<Dog> be passed where an Array<Animal> is expected, and the receiving routine stores a Cat into it. What has the type system permitted?
quiz.answer: An unsound covariant array store, caught only by a run-time check
choices: An unsound covariant array store, caught only by a run-time check
A contravariant parameter position, which is always safe
A generic instantiation that is erased at compile time
A widening conversion that silently copies the array
quiz.explain: Mutable containers must be invariant: covariance is safe for reading and unsafe for writing, which is why such languages need a run-time store check.

quiz.prompt: Hindley-Milner inference is run on  fun f -> fun x -> f (f x). Which type does it produce?
quiz.explain: Applying f to its own result forces f's argument and result types to unify, so f must map a type to itself.

quiz.prompt: Beta-reduce the term (lambda x. lambda y. x) A B to normal form. How many beta-reduction steps does that take?
quiz.explain: One step substitutes A for x, leaving (lambda y. A) B; a second step discards B and yields A.

quiz.prompt: A lazily evaluated program returns a value that, when eventually forced, tries to read from a file the program has already closed. Which property of the language explains the surprise?
quiz.answer: Evaluation order is not tied to the order of the source text
choices: Evaluation order is not tied to the order of the source text
Lazy languages evaluate each argument twice
Closures are unable to capture file handles
Side effects are forbidden in a lazy language
quiz.explain: Laziness defers work to the point of demand, so an effect written before the close can in fact run after it unless the value is forced first.

lesson_media.alt: The typed lambda term lambda x of integer type, x plus 1, applied to 4 is type-checked, substitutes 4 for x, and reduces in one arithmetic step to integer 5.
lesson_media.caption: A type judgment predicts which terms may be evaluated, while operational semantics defines each reduction step. For this term, substitution preserves the integer type and evaluation produces five.

nodes.title: Quantum Computing
nodes.goal: Qubits, gates, and algorithms that change the rules.

quiz.prompt: Unlike a classical bit, a qubit can be in a superposition. What does this mean?
quiz.answer: A combination of 0 and 1 that collapses when measured
quiz.explain: A qubit's state is a superposition with complex amplitudes; measurement yields 0 or 1 probabilistically, collapsing the state.
choices: A combination of 0 and 1 that collapses when measured
It permanently holds both 0 and 1 as outputs at once
It rests exactly halfway between 0 and 1 whenever it is read
It can store any real number directly as its value

quiz.prompt: Shor's algorithm is significant because it can efficiently:
quiz.answer: Factor large integers, threatening RSA encryption
quiz.explain: Factoring has hidden periodic structure that a quantum Fourier transform exposes, which is a specific win rather than a general one. Factoring is not known to be NP-complete, symmetric ciphers lose only a square root of their key strength, and Grover's unstructured search is quadratic rather than exponential.
choices: Factor large integers, threatening RSA encryption
Solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time
Break any cipher, symmetric ciphers like AES included
Search an unsorted collection exponentially faster

quiz.prompt: The no-cloning theorem says no operation can copy an arbitrary unknown qubit state. A student objects that they have just made a second copy of a qubit they prepared themselves in the state |0>. Is that a counterexample?
quiz.answer: No: a known state can simply be prepared twice
quiz.explain: The theorem forbids one operation that copies an arbitrary unknown state. When you know the state you re-prepare it from the description instead of copying the qubit, and orthogonal states can be distinguished and duplicated exactly. This is why error correction cannot lean on a majority vote over copies.
choices: No: a known state can simply be prepared twice
No: the copy is only ever approximate, never exact
No: |0> is a classical value, not a real quantum state
Yes: a qubit prepared by hand was still duplicated

quiz.prompt: Grover's algorithm searches an unstructured space of N items in about the square root of N steps. For N = 1,048,576, give the approximate number of steps.
quiz.explain: The square root of 2^20 is 2^10 = 1,024 oracle queries, against roughly 500,000 classically - a quadratic speedup, not an exponential one.

quiz.prompt: A student prepares a qubit in an equal superposition, measures it, then applies a Hadamard gate and measures again, hoping to recover the state from before the first measurement. Why does this fail?
quiz.answer: The measurement collapsed the state, discarding its phase
choices: The measurement collapsed the state, discarding its phase
The measurement returned a random bit, which the gate cannot use
Measurement is reversible, so the state could be restored later
The Hadamard has to be applied twice to invert itself
quiz.explain: Measurement projects the qubit onto a basis state and throws away the relative phase of the amplitudes. It is not a unitary and cannot be undone, so no later gate - applied once or twice - restores information that has gone.

quiz.prompt: A team runs a 50-qubit circuit of depth 400 on hardware with 0.5% error per two-qubit gate, and the results look like noise. Which explanation matches those numbers?
quiz.answer: Accumulated gate error swamps the signal well before the circuit ends
choices: Accumulated gate error swamps the signal well before the circuit ends
Fifty qubits exceed what a classical computer can simulate
Superposition decays whenever a qubit is measured mid-circuit
The circuit needs more qubits than gates to produce a signal
quiz.explain: Thousands of two-qubit gates at 0.5% error each leave almost no chance of an error-free run, which is why fault-tolerant error correction, not just more qubits, is the bottleneck.

quiz.prompt: A student proposes signalling faster than light by measuring one half of an entangled pair and having a distant partner read the correlated outcome. Why does the scheme fail?
quiz.answer: Each side's outcomes look random until the results are compared
choices: Each side's outcomes look random until the results are compared
The distant qubit is set by the basis you choose, and that is the signal
Measurement takes longer than light needs to cross the distance
Entanglement breaks down beyond a few kilometres of separation
quiz.explain: The correlation shows up only once the two records are brought together over a classical channel, which light speed limits. Choosing a basis changes what you learn, not what the distant partner sees: their marginal statistics are the same whatever you do.

quiz.prompt: A register of 10 qubits is in a general superposition. How many complex amplitudes are needed to describe its state?
quiz.explain: A state over n qubits has one amplitude per basis state, and 2^10 = 1,024.

quiz.prompt: A team wants a logical qubit that survives noise and proposes keeping three copies and taking a majority vote, as with classical bits. Why can they not?
quiz.answer: An unknown state cannot be copied, so the code must entangle instead
choices: An unknown state cannot be copied, so the code must entangle instead
A vote needs the three copies measured, which destroys them
Three copies detect an error but cannot say which copy is wrong
Bit-flip and phase-flip errors cancel, so the vote always ties
quiz.explain: No-cloning blocks the scheme before it starts: nothing produces three copies of an unknown state to vote on. Real codes spread one logical qubit across several physical ones and measure only syndromes, which reveal the error without revealing - and so without destroying - the state.

quiz.prompt: A manager asks whether buying a quantum computer will speed up the company's nightly sort of a customer database. Which answer is correct?
quiz.answer: No: the known quantum speedups need structure that sorting lacks
choices: No: the known quantum speedups need structure that sorting lacks
Yes: Grover's algorithm sorts in the square root of the classical time
Only if the database is first loaded into quantum memory
Yes: superposition lets every comparison be made at once
quiz.explain: Comparison sorting already sits near its classical lower bound of n log n. Grover speeds unstructured search rather than sorting, loading n records into a quantum memory already costs n, and superposition does not hand back the result of every comparison at once - a measurement returns one outcome.

lesson_media.alt: An ideal qubit starts in state zero, one Hadamard gate creates equal positive zero and one amplitudes, and a second Hadamard makes the one-path amplitudes cancel so measurement returns zero.
lesson_media.caption: Quantum gates transform amplitudes, including their signs or phases. Applying H twice is the identity: constructive interference restores the amplitude of state zero and destructive interference cancels state one.

nodes.title: Research Frontiers
nodes.goal: AI alignment, verification and open problems.
articles: List of unsolved problems in computer science

quiz.prompt: The AI alignment problem is fundamentally concerned with:
quiz.answer: Ensuring an AI reliably pursues its designers' goals
quiz.explain: Alignment is about which objective a capable system actually pursues. That is a different problem from raising capability, from stopping deliberate misuse by a human, and from the narrower question of whether stated reasoning matches the answer given.
choices: Ensuring an AI reliably pursues its designers' goals
Making an AI capable enough to be useful in the first place
Preventing an AI from being misused by a hostile operator
Keeping an AI's stated reasoning consistent with its answers

quiz.prompt: Formal verification proves a program meets its specification. Compared to testing, its distinctive strength is:
quiz.answer: It proves a class of bugs absent for all inputs
quiz.explain: A proof covers the properties the specification states, over every input - but only those properties, and only if the specification says what you meant. Writing that specification and discharging the proof obligations is most of the work.
choices: It proves a class of bugs absent for all inputs
It proves the program has no bugs of any kind
It checks that the specification itself is right
It needs no extra work beyond writing the code

quiz.prompt: The P versus NP question appears on lists of major unsolved problems in computer science. Its current status is:
quiz.answer: It remains open; no proof either way exists
quiz.explain: No proof exists in either direction. Decades without a fast algorithm is evidence, not a proof; the question is one question about two classes rather than a problem-by-problem tally; and nothing has shown it undecidable.
choices: It remains open; no proof either way exists
It was proved undecidable, like the halting problem
It is settled in practice, since no fast algorithm was ever found
It is open for only a handful of remaining NP problems

quiz.prompt: A reinforcement-learning agent told to maximise a cleaning robot's 'dust collected' score learns to tip the bin over and vacuum the same dust again. Name the failure mode and say what the score got wrong.
quiz.answer: Reward hacking: the proxy reward counted dust collected instead of how clean the room stayed, so the agent optimised the proxy rather than the intended goal.
quiz.explain: Specification gaming happens when a measurable proxy comes apart from the intended objective, and a capable optimiser finds the gap - which is why reward design and oversight matter.

quiz.prompt: A model scores 92% on a public benchmark but 61% on a freshly written test of the same skill. Which explanation should be investigated first?
quiz.answer: Benchmark items leaked into the training data
choices: Benchmark items leaked into the training data
The fresh test uses harder vocabulary than the benchmark
The model was evaluated with a different random seed
The benchmark rewards longer answers than the fresh test
quiz.explain: Contamination is the leading explanation for a large gap between a public benchmark and a freshly authored one, which is why held-out evaluations matter.

quiz.prompt: A team proves its compiler correct in Coq, yet a program that compiler produced still misbehaves in production. Which possibility does the proof leave open?
quiz.answer: The specification or the trusted runtime outside the proof is wrong
choices: The specification or the trusted runtime outside the proof is wrong
Coq proofs hold for small inputs and lapse on larger ones
The proof checks syntax but leaves semantics unchecked
Machine-checked proofs lapse once the compiler is rebuilt
quiz.explain: A verification result is only as strong as its specification and its trusted computing base, so bugs migrate into the spec, the assumptions or the unverified parts.

quiz.prompt: An audit finds a hiring model with high accuracy whose behaviour on a protected group nobody can account for. Which line of research addresses that gap most directly?
quiz.answer: Mechanistic interpretability of the model's internal computation
choices: Mechanistic interpretability of the model's internal computation
Enlarging the training set until the group's error rate matches the others
Reporting confidence intervals around the accuracy figure
Distilling the model into a smaller one that runs faster
quiz.explain: The complaint is about explanation, not accuracy, so the response has to be a method that opens up how the decision is computed.

quiz.prompt: A hospital's sepsis model degrades sharply after a change of laboratory supplier shifts the calibration of one assay. The inputs have moved; the underlying biology has not. Which response follows from that distinction?
quiz.answer: Recalibrate that feature and revalidate
choices: Recalibrate that feature and revalidate
Retrain on the old data with stronger regularisation
Relabel the historical outcomes to match the new assay
Leave the model alone, since the relationship it learned still holds
quiz.explain: Only the input distribution moved, so the fix belongs at the input: map the new assay onto the scale the model was trained on, or retrain on data from the new supplier, then measure again. That the learned relationship still holds is why the model is worth rescuing, not a reason to do nothing, and the outcomes were never mislabelled.

quiz.prompt: A model produces long technical answers that no human reviewer can check end to end. Which approach is designed for exactly that difficulty?
quiz.answer: Have models critique each other so a human judges the critique
choices: Have models critique each other so a human judges the critique
Check only the final conclusion, which a human can verify quickly
Have a larger model grade the answers with no human in the loop
Cap answer length so that a reviewer can read all of it
quiz.explain: Scalable oversight keeps the human in the loop by decomposing the judgement rather than removing the human or shrinking the task. Checking only the conclusion fails exactly when the error hides in the reasoning, and a model grader with no human has nothing anchoring it to the truth.

quiz.prompt: A benchmark's test items are published openly, and reported scores jump twenty points in a year. Which check best separates genuine progress from contamination?
quiz.answer: Evaluate on a set written after the models' training cutoff
choices: Evaluate on a set written after the models' training cutoff
Check whether the benchmark items appear verbatim in a web corpus
Compare each model's score against the size of its training set
Re-run the public benchmark with a different random seed
quiz.explain: Only data the model cannot have trained on separates capability from memorisation. Searching a corpus helps but covers only the corpora you can search, and much training data is not public; a reseed changes nothing about what was memorised.

lesson_media.alt: A research loop translates a safety claim into a formal specification, verifies a bounded model, tests the running system adversarially, and feeds any counterexample back into the claim and design.
lesson_media.caption: Verification can prove a specified property of a model under explicit assumptions; testing samples behavior of an implementation. Neither alone settles alignment, specification quality, or behavior outside the model.
